raw: A 28-year-old has an open tibial shaft fracture. After debridement there is extensive soft-tissue loss with periosteal stripping and exposed bone that needs a rotational flap. Distal pulses are normal. Gustilo–Anderson type?

IIIB means extensive soft-tissue loss with periosteal stripping and exposed bone, usually needing flap cover. IIIA is high-energy but has adequate soft-tissue cover. IIIC has an arterial injury that needs repair, regardless of the soft tissues.
A 72-year-old independent, cognitively intact woman who walks without aids has a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture (Garden IV). Best treatment?

Displaced intracapsular fractures in older patients have high non-union and AVN rates after fixation. In active, independent, cognitively intact patients, THA gives better function and fewer reoperations than hemiarthroplasty. Fixation is mainly for younger patients.
A Holstein–Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft. The structure at greatest risk is the:

At the distal third the radial nerve is tethered as it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, so it can be stretched or trapped by the fragment. Most radial palsies with closed shaft fractures are neuropraxias that recover.
In staged management of a high-energy tibial pilon fracture, a positive 'wrinkle sign' indicates:
The soft tissues are ready for definitive internal fixation
Deep infection beneath the external fixator

The standard is span (external fixator, often with fibular fixation), scan, then plan. Definitive ORIF waits until swelling settles, often 1–3 weeks. Return of skin wrinkles shows the oedema has resolved enough for safe incisions.
A Schatzker type IV tibial plateau fracture is clinically important because it:
Is a pure lateral split seen in young adults
Involves the medial plateau and often behaves as a fracture-dislocation with vascular or peroneal nerve injury
Is a pure depression of the lateral plateau in osteoporotic bone

Type IV is a high-energy medial plateau fracture that behaves like a knee fracture-dislocation, so check pulses, ankle–brachial index and the peroneal nerve. Type III is pure lateral depression; type VI has metaphyseal–diaphyseal dissociation.
After a crush injury, the pelvis AP view shows pubic symphysis diastasis of 3.5 cm. CT shows widening of the anterior SI joint with intact posterior SI ligaments. Young–Burgess classification?

APC II is symphyseal diastasis (usually more than 2.5 cm) with disruption of the anterior SI, sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments, while the posterior SI ligaments are intact: rotationally unstable, vertically stable. APC III adds posterior SI ligament disruption.
Coronal-plane fracture of a femoral condyle
Fracture of the posterior tibial plateau rim

It is a coronal fracture of the posterior femoral condyle, lateral more often than medial. It is easily missed on the AP view, so get CT. Fixation uses anteroposterior or posteroanterior lag screws; a lateral plate alone does not hold it.
In Denis' three-column model, the middle column consists of the:
Anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior half of the vertebral body
Posterior longitudinal ligament, posterior annulus and posterior wall of the vertebral body
Facet capsules, ligamentum flavum and interspinous ligament

Anterior column: ALL, anterior annulus and anterior half of the body. Middle: PLL, posterior annulus and posterior half of the body. Posterior: the posterior bony arch and ligamentous complex. Two-column injury suggests instability.
Using the Thoracolumbar Injury Classification and Severity Score (TLICS), surgery is generally recommended when the total score is:
TLICS adds injury morphology, posterior ligamentous complex integrity and neurological status. A score of 3 or less suggests non-operative care, 4 is either, and 5 or more suggests surgery.
A belted rear-seat passenger has a horizontal fracture through the L2 spinous process, lamina, pedicles and vertebral body. The most important associated injury to exclude is:

This is a Chance (flexion-distraction) fracture from a lap belt, which is strongly associated with intra-abdominal hollow viscus injury. Calcaneal fractures go with axial-load burst fractures from falls.
Traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (hangman's fracture) is a fracture of the:

It is a bilateral fracture through the C2 pars interarticularis from hyperextension and axial load. The Levine–Edwards classification guides treatment; type IIA (flexion-distraction) should not be treated with traction.
Which odontoid fracture has the highest non-union rate with non-operative treatment?
Type II through the waist has poor blood supply and a small contact area. Non-union risk rises with age over 50, displacement over 5 mm, posterior displacement and angulation.
A 13-year-old girl has adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Which finding warrants MRI of the whole spine?
Mild rib hump on Adams forward bend test

Typical AIS is a right thoracic curve. A left thoracic curve, rapid progression, painful curve, abnormal neurology or abdominal reflexes, or juvenile onset raise suspicion of syrinx, Chiari malformation or tethered cord.
The most common pattern of vertebral involvement in spinal tuberculosis is:

Paradiscal involvement starts in the metaphysis beside the end plate and spreads to the disc and adjacent vertebra. The central type can mimic a tumour and collapse to vertebra plana; the anterior type spreads under the anterior longitudinal ligament.
The most common and consistent finding in cauda equina syndrome from a large central lumbar disc prolapse is:

Urinary retention (often with overflow) is the most common finding, along with saddle anaesthesia and bilateral sciatica. Upper motor neuron signs point to cord compression above the conus. Treat with urgent MRI and decompression.
Lewinnek's 'safe zone' for acetabular cup position is:
Lewinnek described inclination of 30–50° and anteversion of 5–25°. Many dislocations still occur within this zone, so spinopelvic mobility is now also considered when planning cup position.
Which is a major criterion for periprosthetic joint infection under the MSIS/ICM definitions?
A sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis

Major criteria are a sinus tract communicating with the joint, or two positive cultures of the same organism. Serum CRP, ESR and D-dimer, synovial WBC, neutrophil percentage, alpha-defensin and leukocyte esterase are minor criteria.
A periprosthetic femoral fracture around the stem of a THA shows a loose stem with good proximal bone stock (Vancouver B2). Best treatment:
ORIF with a locking plate, retaining the stem
Revision to a long distal-fixation stem, with fracture fixation as needed

B1 (stable stem) is treated with ORIF. B2 (loose stem, good bone) needs revision to a long stem that bypasses the fracture. B3 (loose stem, poor bone) needs revision with structural graft or a megaprosthesis.
During TKA, the extension gap is balanced but the flexion gap is tight. Most appropriate correction:
Downsize the femoral component in the anteroposterior plane

A problem in flexion only is corrected at the posterior femoral condyles (downsize the femur) or by increasing tibial slope. Distal femoral resection and posterior capsular release affect extension; changing the insert affects both gaps.
Periprosthetic osteolysis after hip arthroplasty is mainly driven by:
Macrophage response to submicron polyethylene particles
Polyethylene particles of about 0.1–1 µm are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 and RANKL. These activate osteoclasts and cause bone resorption around the implant.
Three weeks after TKA, a patient has acute pain and swelling. Implants are well fixed and the aspirate grows Staphylococcus aureus. Best treatment:
DAIR with exchange of the modular polyethylene insert

Early postoperative infection (within about 4 weeks) or acute haematogenous infection with stable implants is managed with debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR) with modular exchange. Chronic infection needs one- or two-stage revision.
On knee MRI, a 'double PCL sign' indicates:
Bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus
Hypertrophy of the ligament of Humphrey

The displaced fragment lies in the intercondylar notch, anterior and parallel to the PCL. It is usually from the medial meniscus. Related signs are an absent bow-tie and a flipped meniscus. The ligament of Humphrey is a normal meniscofemoral ligament anterior to the PCL.
After a twisting injury, MRI shows bone marrow oedema in the lateral femoral condyle near the terminal sulcus and in the posterolateral tibial plateau. This pattern suggests:
PCL tear from a dashboard injury

These are pivot-shift contusions from anterior tibial subluxation. Patellar dislocation bruises the medial patellar facet and the anterolateral lateral femoral condyle. Dashboard PCL injury bruises the anterior tibia.
A Segond fracture is an avulsion of the:
Medial tibial plateau by the deep MCL
Lateral tibial plateau by the anterolateral capsule or ligament

It is strongly associated with ACL tear and meniscal injury. A reverse Segond (medial) suggests PCL and medial meniscus injury. Fibular head avulsion is the arcuate sign of posterolateral corner injury.
A 22-year-old has recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation, about 25% anteroinferior glenoid bone loss and an engaging Hill–Sachs lesion. Best procedure:

Critical glenoid bone loss (classically 20–25%, lower in high-demand athletes) needs a bony procedure. Bankart repair alone has a high failure rate here, and remplissage addresses only the humeral side.
The most common type of SLAP lesion is:

Snyder type II is detachment of the superior labrum and biceps anchor. Type I is degenerative fraying, type III is a bucket-handle tear with an intact anchor, and type IV is a bucket-handle tear extending into the biceps tendon.
Dial test: more than 10° increased external rotation at 30° of knee flexion but not at 90°. This indicates:
Combined PCL and posterolateral corner injury
Increased rotation only at 30° indicates an isolated posterolateral corner injury. Increase at both 30° and 90° indicates a combined PCL and posterolateral corner injury.
A meniscal tear has the best healing potential in the:
Radial root tear in an older patient

The peripheral 10–30% of the meniscus is vascularised from the perimeniscal capillary plexus. Repairs heal best in the red–red zone, especially in young patients with acute tears and concurrent ACL reconstruction.
In an acute ACL tear, the meniscus most commonly torn is the:
Neither, as menisci are rarely torn acutely

Lateral meniscal tears are more common with acute ACL injury. In chronic ACL deficiency, medial meniscal tears predominate because the posterior horn of the medial meniscus acts as a secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation.
A 6-week-old being treated in a Pavlik harness for DDH cannot actively extend the knee. Most likely cause:
Sciatic nerve palsy from excessive abduction
Femoral nerve palsy from excessive hip flexion
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

Hyperflexion of the hips can cause femoral nerve palsy, so loosen the anterior straps. Forced abduction risks AVN. If the hip is not reduced within about 3–4 weeks, stop the harness to avoid posterior acetabular wear.
Which combination predicts the worst prognosis in Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease?
Onset under 6 years, lateral pillar A
Onset over 8 years, lateral pillar C
Onset under 6 years, lateral pillar B
Older age at onset (over 8 years) and greater lateral pillar collapse (Herring C) predict a poor outcome. Herring's classification is the most widely used prognostic system.
A 13-year-old obese boy has a stable slipped capital femoral epiphysis and can walk with crutches. Standard treatment:
In situ fixation with a single cannulated screw

In the Loder classification, stable means able to bear weight. Fix in situ with a screw central in the epiphysis and perpendicular to the physis. Forceful reduction increases AVN risk. Klein's line helps detect early slips on AP and frog-lateral views.
In Ponseti correction of idiopathic clubfoot, the first deformity corrected is:

The order is CAVE: cavus first (supinate the forefoot to align it with the hindfoot), then adductus and varus together by abducting around the talar head, and equinus last, usually with percutaneous Achilles tenotomy. A foot abduction brace follows.
The nerve most commonly injured in an extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture is the:

The AIN is most often injured, typically with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment. The radial nerve is at risk with posteromedial displacement. The ulnar nerve is at risk with flexion-type fractures or a medial pin.
A juvenile Tillaux fracture is an avulsion of the:
Anteromedial distal tibial epiphysis by the deltoid ligament
Anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis by the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament
Posterior malleolus by the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament

The distal tibial physis closes centrally, then medially, then laterally, leaving the anterolateral part open in adolescents. The injury is Salter–Harris III; more than 2 mm of displacement usually needs fixation.
Proximal pole AVN after a scaphoid waist fracture occurs because:
The blood supply enters proximally from the ulnar artery
Most of the blood supply is retrograde from dorsal branches of the radial artery entering distal to the waist
The proximal pole is mostly cancellous bone
The scapholunate ligament carries the main supply

About 70–80% of the supply, including all of the proximal pole, comes retrograde from dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery. The distal pole is also supplied by volar branches. A waist fracture cuts the proximal pole off.
Boutonnière deformity results from disruption of the:
Central slip of the extensor mechanism
Volar plate of the DIP joint
Central slip rupture lets the lateral bands sublux volar to the PIP axis, causing PIP flexion and DIP hyperextension. Terminal tendon disruption causes a mallet finger.
Negative ulnar variance is thought to increase load on the lunate. Lichtman staging guides treatment; in early stages with negative variance, radial shortening osteotomy is a common option.
The terrible triad of the elbow consists of:
Posterior dislocation, radial head fracture and coronoid fracture
Anterior dislocation, olecranon fracture and radial head fracture
Posterior dislocation, capitellum fracture and medial epicondyle fracture
Ulnar fracture, PIN palsy and radial head dislocation

The LCL complex is usually avulsed from the lateral epicondyle. Treatment fixes the coronoid, fixes or replaces the radial head, repairs the LCL, and adds MCL repair or a hinged fixator if the elbow is still unstable.
Jersey finger (FDP avulsion) most commonly involves the:
The ring finger is involved in most cases. In the Leddy–Packer classification, type I retracts into the palm with loss of vincular supply, so it should be repaired within about 7–10 days.
Froment's sign tests weakness of the:
With adductor pollicis weak, the patient grips paper by substituting FPL, so the thumb IP joint flexes. Jeanne's sign is the matching hyperextension of the thumb MCP joint.
The most common Bado type of Monteggia lesion is:
Type I, anterior radial head dislocation
Type IV, with radial shaft fracture

Type I (apex-anterior ulnar fracture with anterior radial head dislocation) is the most common, especially in children. The posterior interosseous nerve is most at risk. Type II is relatively more common in adults.
The Lisfranc ligament runs from the:
Medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal
Base of the 1st to the base of the 2nd metatarsal
Intermediate cuneiform to the base of the 1st metatarsal
Navicular to the base of the 2nd metatarsal
Its plantar part is strongest, and there is no intermetatarsal ligament between the 1st and 2nd bases. A 'fleck sign' is an avulsion of the ligament. Get weight-bearing views or CT when suspicious.
The normal Böhler angle on a lateral calcaneal radiograph is about:
A reduced Böhler angle reflects posterior facet depression in intra-articular calcaneal fractures. The critical angle of Gissane is about 120–145°. The Sanders classification is based on coronal CT.
After a talar neck fracture, the Hawkins sign is:
Sclerosis of the talar dome at 6 weeks, indicating AVN
Subchondral lucency of the talar dome at 6–8 weeks, indicating an intact blood supply
Subchondral lucency means disuse osteopenia with revascularisation, a good sign. Its absence does not prove AVN, but a sclerotic dense dome raises concern.
The most common Lauge-Hansen mechanism of ankle fracture is:

SER gives a short oblique fibular fracture at the syndesmosis, running from anteroinferior to posterosuperior (Weber B). Pronation–external rotation gives a high fibular fracture (Weber C, including Maisonneuve).
A fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal (zone 2) is prone to non-union because:
It lies in a vascular watershed
It is always a stress fracture
This is the Jones fracture. Zone 1 avulsions heal well. Zone 3 is the proximal diaphyseal stress fracture. Athletes with zone 2 fractures are often treated with an intramedullary screw.
In hallux valgus assessment, the normal first–second intermetatarsal angle is less than about:
A normal hallux valgus angle is under 15° and a normal IMA under 9°. Larger IMAs usually need a proximal metatarsal osteotomy or a Lapidus procedure rather than a distal osteotomy alone.
Prophylactic fixation of an impending pathological fracture is recommended when the Mirels score is:
Mirels scores site, pain, lesion type and size (1–3 each). A score of 9 or more favours fixation, 7 or less favours radiotherapy and observation, and 8 is a judgement call.
Denosumab treats giant cell tumour of bone by targeting:
Neoplastic stromal cells express RANKL, which recruits osteoclast-like giant cells. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL. Romosozumab targets sclerostin.
Standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy for high-grade osteosarcoma (MAP) consists of:
Histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (90% or more tumour necrosis, Huvos grading) is a major prognostic factor, along with metastases at presentation.
The characteristic translocation in Ewing sarcoma is:
t(X;18) is synovial sarcoma, t(12;16) is myxoid liposarcoma and t(2;13) is alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
Conventional high-grade chondrosarcoma of the pelvis is primarily treated with:

Conventional chondrosarcoma is relatively resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so wide resection is the mainstay. Intralesional curettage is reserved for low-grade lesions (atypical cartilaginous tumour) of the long bones.
A 15-year-old has night pain in the proximal femur relieved by NSAIDs. CT shows a 1 cm lucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis. Treatment of choice:

This is an osteoid osteoma. The nidus is usually under 1.5–2 cm and produces prostaglandins, which explains the NSAID response. CT-guided RFA is first-line when NSAIDs are not tolerated or not wanted long term.
Fracture healing under absolute stability (compression plating) occurs by:
Primary (direct) bone healing by cutting cones
With anatomical reduction and compression, osteoclasts at the front of cutting cones cross the fracture and osteoblasts follow, laying down new osteons without visible callus.
According to Perren's strain theory, interfragmentary strain below about 2% permits:
Strain below 2% allows direct bone formation. Strain of 2–10% allows secondary healing with callus (relative stability). Above 10%, only granulation tissue survives.
In bridge plating, increasing the working length (leaving screw holes empty near the fracture) will:
Decrease construct stiffness and increase interfragmentary motion
Convert healing to primary bone healing
A longer working length spreads strain over more plate and allows more motion, which favours callus. Too short a working length concentrates stress and can lead to plate failure.
Which implant material has an elastic modulus closest to cortical bone?
Cortical bone is about 15–20 GPa, titanium alloy about 110 GPa, stainless steel about 200 GPa, cobalt–chromium over 200 GPa and alumina about 380 GPa. A lower modulus reduces stress shielding.
The predominant collagen in articular hyaline cartilage is:

Type II forms most of the collagen in hyaline cartilage. Type X is found in the hypertrophic zone of the physis and calcified cartilage. Type I dominates in bone, tendon and fibrocartilage repair tissue.
Recombinant BMP-2 has FDA approval for:
Acute open tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing

rhBMP-2 is approved for acute open tibial shaft fractures treated with an IM nail and for certain anterior lumbar interbody fusions. Use in the anterior cervical spine is off-label and linked to dangerous soft-tissue swelling.
The Kocher criteria for distinguishing septic arthritis of the hip from transient synovitis include all EXCEPT:

The four criteria are non-weight-bearing, fever above 38.5 °C, ESR above 40 mm/h and WBC above 12,000/mm³. CRP above 2 mg/dL was added later as a further predictor. Ultrasound shows effusion in both conditions.
A fastidious Gram-negative organism that is a leading cause of osteoarticular infection in children under 4 years, and is often missed on routine culture, is:
Kingella kingae often causes milder inflammatory markers and grows poorly on routine media, so inoculate blood culture bottles or use PCR.
A diabetic patient has a warm, swollen midfoot. Radiographs show fragmentation and the patient is in Eichenholtz stage I Charcot neuroarthropathy. Initial treatment:

The acute fragmentation stage is managed with offloading in a total contact cast until temperature difference and swelling settle. Then move to a CROW walker and later custom footwear. Surgery is reserved for unstable or ulcerating deformity.
Because of an osteosarcoma signal in rat studies, teriparatide is avoided in Paget's disease, open epiphyses, prior skeletal radiation and unexplained raised alkaline phosphatase.
Which radiographic feature suggests an atypical femoral fracture in a patient on long-term bisphosphonates?
Spiral femoral neck fracture after a fall from height
Transverse or short oblique subtrochanteric or diaphyseal fracture with lateral cortical beaking after minimal trauma

Atypical fractures start in the lateral tension cortex. Image the opposite femur as bilateral involvement is common. Stop the bisphosphonate, and treat complete or painful incomplete fractures with an intramedullary nail.
The most common organism causing acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children overall is:
S. aureus, including MRSA in many regions, is the most common cause. Salmonella is classically linked with sickle cell disease and Pseudomonas with puncture wounds through footwear.
Ipsilateral fractures of the femur and tibia
Knee dislocation with popliteal artery injury
Patellar tendon rupture with tibial tubercle avulsion

The knee is disconnected from the rest of the limb by ipsilateral femoral and tibial fractures. Most are high energy, with frequent ligament, vascular and soft-tissue injuries. Both fractures are usually fixed surgically.
The earliest and most reliable clinical feature of acute compartment syndrome in a conscious patient is:
Pain out of proportion to the injury, worse on passive stretch

Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles appear first. Pulselessness and paralysis are late findings, and pulses are often present in established compartment syndrome.
Fasciotomy is generally indicated when the 'delta pressure' (diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure) falls below:
A delta pressure under 30 mmHg indicates compromised perfusion. It is more reliable than an absolute compartment pressure because it accounts for the patient's blood pressure.
In two-incision four-compartment fasciotomy of the leg, the deep posterior compartment is released through the:

The anterolateral incision releases the anterior and lateral compartments. The posteromedial incision, about 2 cm behind the tibial border, releases the superficial and deep posterior compartments; detach soleus from the tibia to reach the deep compartment.
Which is a major criterion in Gurd's criteria for fat embolism syndrome?

Major criteria are petechial rash, respiratory insufficiency and cerebral involvement. Tachycardia, fever, retinal changes, jaundice, renal changes, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, raised ESR and fat macroglobulinaemia are minor.
A polytrauma patient with a femoral shaft fracture is hypothermic, coagulopathic and has a rising lactate. Best initial management of the femur:

In unstable or borderline patients, early total care increases the 'second hit' of systemic inflammation. Damage control means rapid external fixation, resuscitation in ICU, and conversion to definitive nailing once physiology normalises, often after a few days.
A reverse obliquity intertrochanteric fracture is best treated with:
In reverse obliquity fractures, the fracture line runs parallel to the sliding screw, so a DHS allows the shaft to displace medially and has high failure rates. An intramedullary device is preferred.
In fixation of a peritrochanteric fracture with a sliding hip screw, the strongest predictor of lag screw cut-out is a tip–apex distance of more than:
Baumgaertner showed cut-out risk rises sharply above 25 mm. Aim for a central-central or centre-inferior screw position deep in the head on both AP and lateral views.
A 35-year-old has a femoral neck fracture whose line is 60° to the horizontal. Pauwels type and its significance:
Type III, vertical shear with high risk of non-union and fixation failure

Pauwels type III (above 50°) fractures in young adults have high shear forces. They need urgent anatomical reduction and a construct that resists shear, such as a fixed-angle device or added medial support.
In ipsilateral femoral neck and shaft fractures, the component most often missed is the:

The neck fracture is often undisplaced, vertical and basicervical, and is missed in a significant proportion. Get a dedicated hip CT or fine-cut pelvic CT in every femoral shaft fracture, and check the hip again after fixation.
A distal radius fracture with volar displacement and volar angulation of the distal fragment is a:

Smith fracture is a 'reverse Colles'. It is usually unstable in a cast and is commonly treated with a volar buttress plate. Chauffeur's is a radial styloid fracture; die-punch is a depressed lunate facet fracture.
A volar Barton fracture is best treated with:
It is an intra-articular volar rim fracture with volar subluxation of the carpus, which is inherently unstable. A volar buttress plate holds the rim and prevents the carpus from sliding.
In distal radius fractures, surgical fixation is usually advised when the intra-articular step-off exceeds:

Step-off over 2 mm is associated with radiocarpal arthritis. Other commonly cited acceptable limits are radial shortening under 3 mm and dorsal tilt under 10°, though tolerance is greater in low-demand elderly patients.
Proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation
Radial shaft fracture (usually distal third) with DRUJ disruption
Radial head fracture with interosseous membrane tear

In adults, it is treated with ORIF of the radius and then assessment of DRUJ stability. If the DRUJ is unstable, it is pinned in supination or the TFCC is repaired. Proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation is Monteggia.
An Essex-Lopresti injury consists of a radial head fracture together with:
Interosseous membrane disruption and DRUJ injury
Longitudinal forearm instability results. Never excise the radial head, as the radius migrates proximally; fix or replace it, and address the DRUJ.
In the Neer classification of proximal humerus fractures, a segment counts as a 'part' when it is displaced by more than:
Neer's four segments are the head, greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and shaft. Smaller thresholds, such as 5 mm for the greater tuberosity, are often used in practice.
According to Hertel's criteria, which features best predict humeral head ischaemia after a proximal humerus fracture?
Short posteromedial metaphyseal extension (under 8 mm) and a disrupted medial hinge (over 2 mm)
Surgical neck fracture with intact medial hinge
Short calcar extension and a disrupted medial hinge, especially with an anatomical neck fracture, strongly predict ischaemia. Valgus-impacted fractures often keep their blood supply.
Which feature most favours operative fixation of a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture in an adult?
Shortening over 2 cm or skin tenting

Shortening over about 2 cm, complete displacement, skin tenting, open fracture, neurovascular injury and floating shoulder are common indications. Fixation reduces non-union and symptomatic malunion in displaced fractures.
A 'floating shoulder' is usually defined as:
Ipsilateral clavicle and scapular neck fractures
It is a double disruption of the superior shoulder suspensory complex. Scapulothoracic dissociation is a separate, often limb-threatening injury.
A displaced, non-comminuted transverse olecranon fracture in an adult is most commonly treated with:
Tension band wiring converts the triceps' tensile force into compression at the articular surface. Comminuted or oblique fractures, and those extending distal to the coronoid, need plate fixation.
The 'spur sign' on an obturator oblique view of the pelvis is pathognomonic of which acetabular fracture?
In an associated both-column fracture, no part of the articular surface remains attached to the axial skeleton. The spur is the intact part of the iliac wing above the acetabulum.
The obturator oblique (Judet) view best shows the:
The obturator oblique view shows the anterior column and posterior wall. The iliac oblique view shows the posterior column and anterior wall.
After a posterior hip dislocation, the nerve most often injured and the key urgent step are:
Femoral nerve; delayed reduction after 48 hours
Sciatic nerve (peroneal division); reduction as soon as possible, ideally within 6 hours
Superior gluteal nerve; traction for 6 weeks

The peroneal division is more vulnerable as it is tethered at the fibular neck. Early reduction lowers the risk of AVN. Get CT after reduction to look for femoral head fractures, loose bodies and posterior wall fractures.
A femoral head fracture below the fovea with a posterior hip dislocation is Pipkin type:
Type I is below the fovea and type II above it. Type III adds a femoral neck fracture and type IV an acetabular fracture.
Stress fracture of the femoral neck
Closed degloving injury separating subcutaneous fat from the underlying fascia
Avulsion of the anterior inferior iliac spine

It occurs most often over the greater trochanter in pelvic trauma. MRI shows a fluid collection between fat and fascia. It carries a high infection risk if incisions pass through it, so drain or debride it before or during fixation.
A patellar fracture can be treated non-operatively when the extensor mechanism is intact and:
Displacement is under 3 mm and articular step-off under 2 mm
There is an extensor lag of 20°
It is a comminuted inferior pole fracture with lag
Operative indications include loss of active extension, fragment separation over 3 mm, articular step-off over 2 mm and open fractures.
The most common complication after intramedullary nailing of a tibial shaft fracture is:

Anterior knee pain affects a large proportion of patients, partly related to the entry portal and a prominent nail. Suprapatellar nailing in semi-extension aims to reduce this and makes proximal fractures easier to reduce.
When nailing a proximal-third tibial shaft fracture, the classic malalignment is:
Patellar tendon pull and a medial entry point cause valgus and apex-anterior angulation. Prevent it with a lateral entry point, blocking (Poller) screws, semi-extended nailing or temporary plating.
Systemic antibiotics for an open fracture should ideally be started:
Within 1 hour of injury or presentation

Early antibiotics are among the strongest factors in reducing infection. Standard guidance, such as BOAST, recommends giving them within 1 hour of injury or as soon as possible, along with tetanus prophylaxis.
Adequate biology but inadequate stability; needs more stable fixation

Plenty of callus shows the biology is good and motion is the problem. Stable compression fixation, such as exchange nailing or compression plating, usually leads to union without graft. Atrophic non-union needs both biology and stability.
ASIA Impairment Scale grade B means:
Complete loss of motor and sensory function, including S4–S5
Sensory but not motor function preserved below the level, including S4–S5
Motor function preserved, with more than half of key muscles below grade 3

A is complete, B is sensory incomplete, C is motor incomplete with more than half of key muscles below grade 3, D has at least half at grade 3 or more, and E is normal. Sacral sparing defines incompleteness.
A 70-year-old with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hits his forehead. He has weakness, worse in the hands than the legs, with sacral sparing. Most likely diagnosis:

Hyperextension in a spondylotic canal injures the central grey matter and medial corticospinal fibres, which serve the upper limbs. It is the most common incomplete cord syndrome, with fair recovery; hand function recovers least.
Bilateral loss of pain and temperature
Ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss with contralateral loss of pain and temperature
Contralateral motor loss with ipsilateral pain loss
It results from cord hemisection, often from penetrating injury. It has the best prognosis of the incomplete cord syndromes.
Which incomplete spinal cord syndrome carries the worst prognosis for motor recovery?
Anterior cord syndrome, from flexion injury or anterior spinal artery ischaemia, causes motor and pain-temperature loss with preserved proprioception. It has the poorest motor recovery.
The end of spinal shock is marked by the return of the:
The bulbocavernosus reflex usually returns within 48 hours. A patient with no sacral sparing once it returns has a complete injury.
A patient with a cervical cord injury has hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is:

Loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation and unopposed vagal bradycardia. Spinal shock is the loss of reflexes below the injury, not a circulatory state. Exclude bleeding before attributing hypotension to neurogenic shock.
On an open-mouth odontoid view of a C1 burst (Jefferson) fracture, combined lateral mass overhang of more than about 7 mm suggests:
Spence's rule (about 6.9 mm, with radiographic magnification) suggests a torn transverse ligament and instability. MRI now confirms ligament integrity directly.
The normal atlanto-dens interval in an adult is less than:
Under 3 mm in adults and under 5 mm in children. A widened interval suggests transverse ligament insufficiency, as in rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome or trauma.
A Powers ratio greater than 1 suggests:
The ratio of basion–posterior arch distance to opisthion–anterior arch distance is normally under 1. A ratio over 1 indicates anterior occipitocervical dislocation.
On a lateral cervical radiograph, about 25% anterior translation of one vertebral body on the next suggests:

About 25% translation suggests a unilateral facet dislocation; about 50% suggests a bilateral facet dislocation, which has a high rate of cord injury. Get MRI to look for disc herniation before reduction in patients who cannot cooperate with examination.
A clay-shoveler's fracture is an avulsion fracture of the:
It is caused by muscle pull or direct flexion force on the lower cervical spinous process. It is stable and treated symptomatically.
On oblique lumbar radiographs, a 'collar on the Scottie dog' indicates:
The Scottie dog's neck is the pars. Spondylolysis is most common at L5. CT or MRI is more sensitive, and MRI or SPECT can show an early stress reaction.
In Meyerding grading of spondylolisthesis, grade II is a slip of:
Grade I is up to 25%, II 26–50%, III 51–75%, IV 76–100%, and grade V (spondyloptosis) is more than 100%.
Isthmic spondylolisthesis of L5 on S1 most commonly compresses the:

The L5 root, which exits at L5–S1, is trapped in the foramen by the fibrocartilaginous pars mass and the slip. In degenerative L4–5 listhesis, the traversing L5 root is compressed in the lateral recess.
A posterolateral L4–L5 disc prolapse typically compresses the:
A posterolateral disc compresses the traversing root, which exits one level below (L5 at L4–5). A far lateral (foraminal or extraforaminal) disc compresses the exiting root (L4 at L4–5).
A far lateral (extraforaminal) L4–L5 disc herniation most commonly produces:
L4 radiculopathy with reduced knee reflex
S1 radiculopathy with absent ankle reflex
A far lateral disc compresses the exiting L4 root, causing anterior thigh and medial leg pain, quadriceps weakness and a reduced knee reflex. Approach it via a paramedian Wiltse route.
Isolated weakness of extensor hallucis longus with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot points to which root?

L5 supplies EHL, hip abduction and the dorsum of the foot, and has no reliable reflex. S1 gives ankle reflex, plantarflexion and lateral foot sensation; L4 gives the knee reflex and medial leg sensation.
Which feature best distinguishes neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication?
Pain in the calves on walking
Relief by sitting or bending forward, with symptoms on standing still
Lumbar flexion widens the canal ('shopping cart sign'), so patients can cycle but not walk uphill comfortably. Vascular claudication eases with standing still and has a fixed walking distance.
Modic type 1 end-plate changes on MRI appear:
Type 1 is bone marrow oedema and the most associated with active low back pain. Type 2 is fatty replacement (T1 and T2 bright) and type 3 is sclerosis (dark on both).
In cervical OPLL, a K-line (–) means:
Laminoplasty alone is likely to give good decompression
The ossified mass projects beyond the K-line, so posterior laminoplasty alone gives poor decompression

The K-line joins the midpoints of the canal at C2 and C7. When OPLL crosses it (K-line negative), the cord cannot drift back enough after laminoplasty, so anterior decompression or posterior fusion is preferred.
In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, surgical correction is generally recommended when the Cobb angle exceeds about:
Curves over 45–50° tend to progress even after maturity. Bracing is typically used for 20/25–40° curves in skeletally immature patients (Risser 0–2).
The Risser sign assesses skeletal maturity by:
Ossification of the iliac crest apophysis
Fusion of the distal radial physis
Closure of the triradiate cartilage only
Grades 0–5 follow the iliac apophysis from lateral to medial. Low Risser grade and premenarchal status mean higher risk of curve progression.
Scheuermann kyphosis is defined radiographically by:
Wedging of at least 5° in three or more consecutive vertebrae
Sorensen's criteria are wedging of 5° or more in at least three adjacent vertebrae. End-plate irregularity and Schmorl nodes are common. Kyphosis over about 75° in an adolescent may need surgery.
Which congenital scoliosis anomaly carries the worst prognosis for progression?
Unilateral unsegmented bar with contralateral hemivertebra

It combines a growth tether on one side with an extra growth centre on the other, causing rapid progression. Early surgery is usually needed. Screen for cardiac, renal and intraspinal anomalies, such as with MRI.
A man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis falls from standing height and has new neck pain but normal radiographs. Next step:
CT of the whole spine, with MRI if needed

The fused osteoporotic spine fractures like a long bone, often through all three columns, and fractures are easily missed on radiographs. Non-contiguous fractures occur, so image the whole spine. Never force the neck into neutral; immobilise in the patient's usual posture.
Early destruction of the intervertebral disc space with end-plate erosion on MRI favours:

Pyogenic organisms produce proteolytic enzymes that destroy the disc early. TB lacks these enzymes and tends to preserve the disc until later and causes large, thin-walled paravertebral abscesses with subligamentous spread. Metastases usually spare the disc.
In the 'middle path regimen' for spinal tuberculosis, surgery is indicated mainly for:
Neurological deficit that fails to improve or worsens despite antitubercular therapy
A paravertebral abscess on MRI alone
Most patients do well on antitubercular drugs alone. Other indications are severe or progressive kyphosis, instability, failure to respond to drugs, and diagnostic doubt needing biopsy.
Rajasekaran's 'spine-at-risk' radiological signs in childhood spinal TB predict:

The signs are facet separation, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation and toppling. Children with two or more signs are at risk of severe kyphosis progression with growth and may need early surgery.
Prostate cancer spreads to the lumbar spine mainly via:

Batson's plexus has no valves, so rises in intra-abdominal pressure push blood, and tumour cells, from the pelvic veins into the vertebral veins. This explains the common lumbosacral and pelvic spread of prostate and other pelvic cancers.
A Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) of 13 or more indicates:
0–6 is stable, 7–12 indeterminate (possibly impending instability) and 13–18 unstable. SINS considers location, pain, lesion type, alignment, collapse and posterolateral involvement.
The 'winking owl' sign on an AP spine radiograph indicates:
Destruction of a pedicle, usually by metastasis
Pedicle destruction usually reflects metastatic disease or myeloma. Infection tends to spare the pedicle early and affects the end plates and disc.
During primary TKA, the knee is tight in both flexion and extension with a trial insert of the thinnest available thickness. The most appropriate correction is to:

A gap problem that is symmetric (tight in both flexion and extension) is corrected on the tibial side, because the tibial cut affects both gaps equally. Distal femoral resection and posterior capsular release change mainly the extension gap; downsizing the femur changes mainly the flexion gap.
In medial release for a fixed varus knee during TKA, which structure is tight mainly in flexion, so that releasing it opens the medial flexion gap more than the extension gap?
Anterior fibres of the superficial MCL

The anterior part of the superficial MCL is taut in flexion, so its release (or pie-crusting) mainly opens the medial flexion gap. The posterior oblique ligament, semimembranosus and posteromedial capsule are tight in extension, so releasing them mainly opens the medial extension gap.
The day after TKA for a severe valgus knee with a fixed flexion contracture, the patient cannot dorsiflex the ankle or extend the toes. The best immediate step is to:
Order an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine
Return to theatre to explore the popliteal artery
Remove the tight dressing and flex the knee

Common peroneal nerve palsy is a recognised risk after correcting valgus with flexion contracture, as the nerve is stretched. Loosening the dressing and flexing the knee to take tension off the nerve is the first step; most palsies are partial and many recover. Holding the knee in extension increases the stretch.
After TKA, the most common component-related cause of lateral patellar maltracking is:
External rotation of the femoral component
Internal rotation of the femoral or tibial component

Internal rotation of either the femoral or tibial component moves the trochlea and tibial tubercle relative to each other and increases the effective Q-angle, causing lateral tracking. Mild external rotation, lateralising the femoral component and medialising the patellar button all improve tracking.

In a valgus knee with a hypoplastic lateral femoral condyle, using the posterior condylar axis to set femoral component rotation tends to cause internal rotation. The most reliable alternative landmark is the:
Whiteside anteroposterior axis or the transepicondylar axis

The posterior condylar axis is normally about 3° internally rotated to the transepicondylar axis and becomes unreliable when the lateral posterior condyle is deficient. Whiteside's line (the trochlear groove to the intercondylar notch) is perpendicular to the transepicondylar axis and is not affected by condylar wear.
Several months after posterior-stabilised TKA, a patient has a painful catch and jump of the patella as the knee extends from about 40° of flexion. Most likely diagnosis:
Patellar clunk syndrome from a suprapatellar fibrous nodule

Patellar clunk is a fibrous nodule at the junction of the quadriceps tendon and superior patellar pole that catches in the intercondylar box of a PS femoral component and then releases as the knee extends. Arthroscopic or open debridement of the nodule is usually curative.
In a posterior-stabilised TKA, the cam-and-post mechanism mainly serves to:
Produce femoral rollback in flexion in place of the PCL
Replace the function of the ACL in extension

The femoral cam engages the tibial post as the knee flexes, forcing the femur to roll back and improving flexion and quadriceps lever arm. It gives little varus–valgus constraint; a constrained condylar or hinged design is needed for collateral insufficiency.
After THA through the posterior approach, which step most reduces the dislocation rate?
Routine use of a 22 mm head
Repair of the posterior capsule and short external rotators

Formal repair of the posterior capsule and short external rotators lowers the dislocation rate after the posterior approach to near that of other approaches. Larger heads increase jump distance and also help; small heads and cup retroversion increase instability.

In the direct lateral (Hardinge) approach to the hip, splitting gluteus medius too far proximally endangers the superior gluteal nerve, which lies about how far above the tip of the greater trochanter?

The superior gluteal nerve runs between gluteus medius and minimus roughly 5 cm above the trochanteric tip, so the split is kept within this 'safe zone'. Injury causes abductor weakness and a Trendelenburg gait.
When sciatic nerve palsy occurs after THA, the division most commonly affected is the:

The peroneal division is more often injured because it is more laterally placed, has fewer and larger fascicles with less connective tissue, and is tethered at the sciatic notch and fibular neck. Excessive limb lengthening and retractor pressure are common causes.
Using Wasielewski's acetabular quadrant system, the safest quadrant for acetabular screw placement is the:

The quadrants are formed by a line from the ASIS through the centre of the acetabulum and a line perpendicular to it. The posterosuperior quadrant is safest; the anterosuperior quadrant risks the external iliac vessels and the anteroinferior quadrant the obturator vessels and nerve. The posteroinferior quadrant risks the sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal vessels with long screws.
Audible squeaking after THA is a complication most characteristic of which bearing couple?

Squeaking occurs mainly with hard-on-hard bearings, especially ceramic on ceramic, and is linked to edge loading from cup malposition. Ceramic bearings also carry a small risk of fracture, but they have the lowest wear rates.
A patient with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing has groin pain and raised serum cobalt and chromium levels. The most useful imaging to look for an adverse local tissue reaction (pseudotumour) is:

MARS MRI (ultrasound is an alternative) shows soft-tissue masses, fluid collections and abductor damage around metal bearings. Management combines symptoms, blood metal ion levels and imaging; a progressive or symptomatic lesion usually needs revision to a non-metal bearing.

Years after a metal-on-polyethylene THA with a cobalt–chromium head on a titanium stem, a patient has new pain and a fluid collection. Taper corrosion (trunnionosis) is suspected. The typical blood metal ion pattern is:
Chromium raised much more than cobalt
Cobalt raised disproportionately more than chromium

Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion at the head–neck taper releases cobalt more than chromium, so a cobalt level rising out of proportion to chromium is typical. Revision involves exchanging the head, often to a ceramic head with a titanium sleeve, after checking the trunnion.
In the manufacture of highly crosslinked polyethylene, melting after irradiation (rather than annealing below the melt temperature):
Leaves residual free radicals but keeps strength
Increases fatigue strength and fracture toughness
Removes residual free radicals but reduces mechanical properties

Irradiation creates crosslinks that improve wear resistance and also free radicals that cause oxidation. Remelting removes the free radicals but reduces crystallinity, fatigue strength and toughness; annealing preserves more mechanical strength but leaves some free radicals. Vitamin E is added to stabilise free radicals without remelting.
Delamination and pitting of older TKA polyethylene inserts were mainly caused by:
Gamma sterilisation in air followed by shelf oxidation

Gamma irradiation in air produced free radicals that reacted with oxygen during storage, causing subsurface oxidation, embrittlement and fatigue failure (delamination). Modern inserts are sterilised in inert gas or vacuum, or by ethylene oxide or gas plasma, and packaged without oxygen.
An elderly woman has a wide, thin-walled 'stovepipe' proximal femoral canal (Dorr type C) and needs a THA. The femoral fixation generally favoured is:

Dorr type C bone has thin cortices and a capacious canal, so a press-fit stem has poor initial stability and a higher risk of intraoperative fracture and subsidence. A cemented stem gives immediate fixation. Dorr type A (champagne flute) suits uncemented fixation.
Which is a first-generation cementing technique rather than a modern (third-generation) one?
Use of a distal cement restrictor and pressurisation

First-generation cementing used hand mixing and finger packing without canal preparation. Second generation added a restrictor, canal cleaning and a cement gun; third generation added vacuum mixing (porosity reduction), pulsatile lavage, pressurisation and stem centralisers.
During cemented hemiarthroplasty for a hip fracture, a 90-year-old suddenly becomes hypoxic and hypotensive as the femoral stem is cemented and inserted. Most likely diagnosis:

Pressurising cement into the canal drives marrow fat, cement particles and debris into the circulation, causing hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia or cardiac arrest. Risk is reduced by careful canal lavage, gentle pressurisation, good communication with the anaesthetist and adequate filling before cementing.
In revision THA, pelvic discontinuity refers to:
A loose cup with contained cavitary defects
Isolated loss of the medial wall
Separation of the superior and inferior halves of the acetabulum through both columns

The ilium is no longer in continuity with the ischium and pubis. On radiographs look for a fracture line through both columns, medial translation of the inferior hemipelvis and rotation of the obturator ring. A standard cup alone fails; options include a cup–cage, acetabular distraction or a custom triflange component.
Brooker grade IV heterotopic ossification after THA means:
Islands of bone in the soft tissues
Spurs leaving more than 1 cm between opposing surfaces
Spurs leaving less than 1 cm between opposing surfaces
Apparent bony ankylosis of the hip

Grade I is islands of bone, II spurs more than 1 cm apart, III less than 1 cm apart, and IV apparent ankylosis. In high-risk patients, prophylaxis is an NSAID such as indomethacin or a single dose of radiation given shortly before or within about 72 hours after surgery.
A patient with a long lumbosacral fusion (a stiff spine with little pelvic tilt between standing and sitting) needs a THA. Which choice most reduces the risk of dislocation?
Routine use of a hip abduction brace for 3 months

A stiff spine prevents the normal posterior pelvic tilt on sitting, so the cup does not gain functional anteversion and anterior impingement with posterior dislocation is more likely. Dual-mobility bearings increase the effective head size and jump distance; small heads and a closed cup worsen instability.
Which of these is a contraindication to Oxford mobile-bearing medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty?
Bone-on-bone medial arthritis with a correctable varus deformity
Patellofemoral osteophytes without lateral facet damage

The Oxford indication for medial UKA is anteromedial osteoarthritis with full-thickness medial cartilage loss, a functionally intact ACL, a correctable deformity and preserved lateral cartilage. ACL deficiency causes posterior tibial wear and bearing instability. Age, weight and isolated patellofemoral osteophytes are no longer regarded as contraindications.
A displaced supracondylar femoral fracture occurs above a well-fixed TKA. In the Rorabeck classification this is type:

Type I is undisplaced with an intact prosthesis, type II is displaced with an intact prosthesis, and type III has a loose or failing prosthesis. Type II is fixed with a distal femoral locking plate or a retrograde nail if the femoral component's box allows; type III needs revision.
Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss in arthroplasty by:
Blocking lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing fibrinolysis
Increasing thrombin generation through vitamin K

Tranexamic acid is a synthetic lysine analogue that stops plasminogen and plasmin binding to fibrin, so clots are not broken down. It reduces transfusion after hip and knee arthroplasty without a clear increase in thromboembolism.
In the Enneking (MSTS) staging of malignant bone tumours, a high-grade osteosarcoma that has broken through the cortex into the soft tissues without metastases is stage:
Stage I is low grade and stage II high grade; A is intracompartmental and B extracompartmental; stage III is any grade with metastasis. Most osteosarcomas present as IIB.
In Enneking's surgical margins, a 'wide' margin means the plane of resection passes:
Through the reactive zone around the tumour
Through normal tissue outside the reactive zone but within the same compartment

Intralesional margins enter the tumour and marginal margins pass through the reactive zone, which may hold satellite lesions. Wide margins keep a cuff of normal tissue around the tumour and reactive zone. Radical margins remove the whole compartment.
A 16-year-old has a suspected primary malignant tumour of the distal femur. Which biopsy principle is correct?
Use a transverse incision for better cosmesis
Place the biopsy tract along the line of the planned resection so it can be excised
Approach through the interval between the vessels and nerves
Use a tourniquet and release it only after the wound is closed

The biopsy tract is contaminated and must be removed with the tumour, so it should be longitudinal, in line with the definitive incision, through a single muscle rather than intermuscular planes, and away from the neurovascular bundle. Achieve haemostasis before closure to avoid haematoma spreading tumour. Ideally the biopsy is done at the treating centre.
A 30-year-old has a densely ossified mass on the posterior surface of the distal femur that wraps around the bone, with a thin lucent line separating it from the cortex. Most likely diagnosis:

Parosteal osteosarcoma is a low-grade surface tumour typical of the posterior distal femur in young adults; the lucent 'string sign' is the cleavage plane. It is treated by wide resection without chemotherapy unless high-grade dedifferentiation is present. Osteochondroma shows continuity of cortex and medulla with the host bone; myositis ossificans matures from the periphery inwards.

MRI of an expansile lytic lesion in a 14-year-old's proximal tibia shows multiple fluid–fluid levels with thick, nodular, enhancing septa and a soft-tissue mass. The diagnosis that must be excluded is:

Fluid–fluid levels occur in aneurysmal bone cyst but also in telangiectatic osteosarcoma. Thick nodular septa, solid enhancing areas, cortical destruction and a soft-tissue mass favour telangiectatic osteosarcoma, so biopsy the solid parts before treating as an ABC.
Primary aneurysmal bone cyst is characterised by a rearrangement of which gene?

Primary ABC is a true neoplasm with USP6 rearrangements (often CDH11–USP6). Secondary ABC change occurs in other lesions such as giant cell tumour, chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma, and lacks the USP6 rearrangement. GNAS is mutated in fibrous dysplasia and IDH1/2 in enchondromas.
A 14-year-old with open physes has a well-defined lytic lesion with a sclerotic rim and fine stippled calcification in the proximal humeral epiphysis. Most likely diagnosis:

Chondroblastoma is the classic epiphyseal tumour of the skeletally immature, often with surrounding oedema on MRI and 'chicken-wire' calcification on histology; it carries an H3F3B K36M mutation. Giant cell tumour is epiphyseal-metaphyseal after physeal closure, and clear cell chondrosarcoma is epiphyseal in adults.
Which feature most suggests a low-grade chondrosarcoma (atypical cartilaginous tumour) rather than an enchondroma in a long bone?
Location in a phalanx of the hand
Deep endosteal scalloping of more than two-thirds of the cortical thickness

Pain unrelated to fracture, deep or extensive endosteal scalloping, cortical thickening or breach, periosteal reaction and a soft-tissue mass favour chondrosarcoma. Ring-and-arc calcification is seen in both, and hand enchondromas rarely become malignant.
Maffucci syndrome differs from Ollier disease by the presence of:

Both have multiple enchondromas, usually from somatic IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, with a substantial risk of chondrosarcoma. Maffucci adds soft-tissue haemangiomas (phleboliths on radiographs) and carries a higher risk of other malignancies.
A 35-year-old with multiple hereditary exostoses has a pelvic osteochondroma that has become larger and painful. On MRI, which finding most suggests secondary chondrosarcoma?
A cartilage cap thicker than 2 cm
A stalk continuous with the medullary canal

In an adult, a cartilage cap over about 1.5–2 cm, growth after skeletal maturity and new pain suggest malignant change, most often in pelvic and shoulder-girdle lesions. Medullary and cortical continuity define any osteochondroma. MHE is caused by EXT1 or EXT2 mutations.
McCune–Albright syndrome consists of polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with:
Café-au-lait spots and endocrine hyperfunction such as precocious puberty
Both result from postzygotic activating GNAS mutations. Café-au-lait spots have irregular 'coast of Maine' borders. Fibrous dysplasia with intramuscular myxomas is Mazabraud syndrome.
A 25-year-old has a multilocular, 'soap-bubble' lytic lesion of the anterior tibial diaphyseal cortex. Biopsy shows epithelial cells that stain for cytokeratin. Diagnosis and treatment:

Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant tumour with a strong predilection for the anterior tibial cortex. Keratin-positive epithelial nests distinguish it from osteofibrous dysplasia, which occurs in younger children. It is resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so wide resection is required.

A 5-year-old has back pain. Radiographs show uniform collapse of a single thoracic vertebral body (vertebra plana) with preserved discs. Biopsy shows cells positive for CD1a and langerin (CD207). Diagnosis:

Langerhans cell histiocytosis is the classic cause of vertebra plana in children; Birbeck granules are seen on electron microscopy. Solitary spinal lesions are usually managed conservatively and often reconstitute height. Infection usually destroys the disc, and Ewing sarcoma tends to form a large soft-tissue mass.

A 10-year-old has a pathological fracture through a central lytic lesion of the proximal humeral metaphysis. A bone fragment lies in the dependent part of the lesion. This 'fallen fragment' sign indicates:

The fragment falls through the fluid-filled cavity, which shows the lesion is hollow and fluid-filled rather than solid. Simple bone cysts are typically central, metaphyseal and in the proximal humerus or femur; ABCs are eccentric, expansile and show fluid–fluid levels.
A 30-year-old has a Campanacci grade II giant cell tumour of the distal femur with a good articular shell. Standard surgical treatment is:
Extended intralesional curettage with a high-speed burr, an adjuvant and cement or graft

Most GCTs around the knee can keep the joint with extended curettage, a high-speed burr, and local adjuvants such as phenol, hydrogen peroxide or argon, followed by PMMA, which also helps detect recurrence. Resection is kept for extensive destruction or unreconstructable articular surfaces.
A 65-year-old has multiple lytic lesions and suspected multiple myeloma. Why is a technetium bone scan unreliable for staging?
Myeloma lesions are always too small
The lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic activity, so they often appear cold
Myeloma does not affect the axial skeleton
Technetium is contraindicated in renal failure
Bone scans depend on osteoblastic activity, which myeloma suppresses, so lesions are often missed. Whole-body low-dose CT, MRI or PET-CT, and the skeletal survey in some centres, are used instead.
Before internal fixation of an impending pathological fracture from a metastasis of renal cell carcinoma in the femoral shaft, the most important preoperative step is:
Bone scan of the whole skeleton only
Radiotherapy to the site the day before surgery

Renal cell and thyroid metastases are highly vascular and can bleed heavily during surgery. Embolisation within a day or two before surgery reduces blood loss. Solitary renal metastases may be considered for wide resection rather than fixation alone.

A 60-year-old has a destructive lytic lesion of the femur and no known cancer. Before biopsy, the recommended initial workup includes history and examination, blood tests including serum protein electrophoresis, and:
CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and a whole-body bone scan

Rougraff's protocol identifies the primary in most cases; lung and kidney are the most frequent sources found. Imaging first may reveal a more accessible biopsy site. A solitary lesion must never be assumed to be a metastasis and fixed before biopsy, because it may be a primary sarcoma.
Which feature of a soft-tissue mass should most prompt referral to a sarcoma centre before any biopsy or excision?
A mass deep to the deep fascia that is larger than 5 cm
A soft mass that has not changed for 10 years

Size over 5 cm, deep location, increasing size and pain are warning signs. Get an MRI and refer for a planned biopsy. 'Whoops' excision of an unsuspected sarcoma contaminates tissue planes and makes limb salvage harder.
Most soft-tissue sarcomas spread by the bloodstream to the lungs. Which subtype is well known for lymph node metastasis?

Lymph node spread is typical of epithelioid, clear cell, synovial, angiosarcoma and rhabdomyosarcoma, so examine and image the nodes in these. Well-differentiated liposarcoma and DFSP rarely metastasise.
A thigh myxoid liposarcoma has been diagnosed. In addition to chest CT, staging should include:
Whole-spine MRI because of a tendency to spread to bone and extrapulmonary sites

Myxoid liposarcoma (FUS–DDIT3, t(12;16)) often spreads to unusual sites such as the spine, retroperitoneum and other soft tissues, and bone metastases may be missed on bone scan or PET. Whole-spine or whole-body MRI is commonly added to staging.
MRI of a swollen knee in a 30-year-old shows nodular synovial thickening with low signal on T1 and T2 that 'blooms' on gradient-echo sequences. Most likely diagnosis:
Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (pigmented villonodular synovitis)

Haemosiderin deposits cause low signal on all sequences with blooming artefact on gradient-echo imaging. The tumour is driven by CSF1 overexpression. Treatment is complete synovectomy; CSF1 receptor inhibitors are used for diffuse, recurrent disease.
Van Nes rotationplasty after resection of a distal femoral sarcoma in a young child works by:
Rotating the leg 180° so the ankle acts as a knee joint
Lengthening the femur with a growing prosthesis
Transferring the fibula to replace the femur

The distal tibia and foot are rotated 180° and attached to the femur, so ankle plantarflexion extends the new 'knee' and dorsiflexion flexes it, with the foot fitted inside a below-knee prosthesis. It gives durable, high function without implant revision as the child grows, at the cost of appearance.
A 60-year-old has a destructive midline sacral mass with soft-tissue extension. Biopsy shows vacuolated physaliferous cells positive for brachyury. Diagnosis:

Chordoma arises from notochordal remnants, mostly in the sacrum and clivus. It is resistant to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy, so en bloc resection with negative margins is the main treatment; high-dose particle therapy is used when resection is not possible.
A vertebral body shows thickened vertical trabeculae ('corduroy' on radiographs, 'polka-dot' on axial CT) and high signal on both T1 and T2 MRI. Most likely diagnosis:

Typical haemangiomas contain fat, so they are bright on T1 and T2, while metastases are usually dark on T1. Most are incidental; aggressive haemangiomas with cord compression may need embolisation, vertebroplasty or surgery. Paget's disease enlarges the vertebra with a 'picture-frame' cortical thickening.
In a newborn hip examination, a positive Barlow test means:
A located hip can be dislocated posteriorly by adduction and gentle posterior pressure
A dislocated hip reduces with abduction and anterior lift
There is limited abduction from a long-standing dislocation
There is apparent shortening of the thigh with the hips and knees flexed

Barlow's test is provocative: it shows a reduced but dislocatable hip. Ortolani's test reduces an already dislocated hip with a clunk. Limited abduction and the Galeazzi sign (apparent femoral shortening) appear later, once the hip is fixed in a dislocated position.
In Graf ultrasound of the infant hip, a mature type I hip has an alpha angle of at least:

The alpha angle measures the slope of the bony acetabular roof against the iliac line. An angle of 60° or more is type I (mature), 50–59° is type II, and below 43° indicates a decentred or dislocated hip (types III and IV). Ultrasound is preferred until the femoral head ossifies at about 4–6 months.
On an AP pelvic radiograph of an infant, where should the ossific nucleus of a normal femoral head lie relative to Hilgenreiner's and Perkins' lines?

Hilgenreiner's line passes horizontally through the triradiate cartilages and Perkins' line drops vertically from the lateral acetabular margin. A normal head lies in the inferomedial quadrant; a dislocated head moves superolaterally and Shenton's line is broken.
Which of the following is NOT a recognised obstacle to closed reduction of a developmentally dislocated hip?

Intra-articular obstacles include an inverted limbus, hypertrophied ligamentum teres, pulvinar and a contracted transverse acetabular ligament. The main extra-articular obstacle is the iliopsoas tendon, which gives the capsule an hourglass constriction. Gluteus maximus does not block reduction.
In Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, which radiographic finding is one of Catterall's 'head-at-risk' signs?
Coxa breva with an intact lateral pillar
Gage sign (a V-shaped lucency in the lateral epiphysis and metaphysis)
Catterall's head-at-risk signs are the Gage sign, lateral calcification, lateral subluxation, a horizontal physis and metaphyseal cysts. They indicate loss of containment and a poorer prognosis.
The Stulberg classification in Perthes disease is based on:
Femoral head shape and its congruency with the acetabulum at skeletal maturity
The extent of epiphyseal necrosis on early radiographs
The height of the lateral pillar during fragmentation

Stulberg classes I–V describe the healed head (spherical, ovoid or flat) and whether it matches the acetabulum, and they predict long-term arthritis, worst in classes IV and V. The Herring lateral pillar and Catterall classifications describe the active disease.
A 9-year-old boy of normal weight has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis. What is the most appropriate additional evaluation?

SCFE outside the usual age range (under 10 or over 16) or in a child who is not obese suggests an endocrine or metabolic cause such as hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency or therapy, or renal osteodystrophy. These slips are more often bilateral, so prophylactic fixation of the other hip is often considered.
An obese 12-year-old with knee pain has obligatory external rotation of the hip when it is passively flexed. This is the:

The Drehmann sign is typical of SCFE: as the hip flexes, the displaced proximal femur is forced into external rotation. Hip disease often presents as referred knee pain, so always examine the hip. The Thomas test detects a fixed flexion deformity.
During Ponseti treatment of idiopathic clubfoot, the foot now abducts to about 60–70° but ankle dorsiflexion stays below 10–15°. The next step is:
Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy, then a final cast for about 3 weeks

Most feet need a tenotomy to correct residual equinus once abduction is adequate, followed by about 3 weeks in a cast and then a foot abduction brace. Tibialis anterior transfer is used for dynamic supination after relapse in older children.
After Ponseti correction of clubfoot, the foot abduction brace is typically worn:
Full time (about 23 hours a day) for about 3 months, then at night and nap times until about 4–5 years of age
Only at night from the start, until walking age
Full time until 2 years of age
Poor brace compliance is the main cause of relapse. The shoe on the affected side is set in about 60–70° of external rotation (about 40° on a normal side), joined by a bar.
A newborn has a rigid rocker-bottom foot. On a lateral radiograph in forced plantarflexion, the talar axis still passes plantar to the first metatarsal axis. Diagnosis:

In congenital vertical talus the navicular is irreducibly dislocated dorsally on the talar neck. In oblique talus the talonavicular joint reduces in plantarflexion, and calcaneovalgus is a positional deformity that resolves. CVT is now often treated with reverse Ponseti-type serial casting and limited surgery.
A 12-year-old has recurrent ankle sprains and a rigid flatfoot. A lateral foot radiograph shows an elongated anterior process of the calcaneus (the 'anteater nose' sign). This suggests:

Calcaneonavicular coalition is best seen on a 45° oblique view and gives the anteater sign on the lateral view. Talocalcaneal (middle facet) coalition gives the C-sign and talar beaking and is best shown on CT. Peroneal spasm with a rigid flatfoot is typical of both.
Most cases of osteogenesis imperfecta result from mutations in genes encoding:

The classic Sillence types I–IV are autosomal dominant defects of type I collagen. Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, COL2A1 mutations cause spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia and Stickler syndrome, and COMP mutations cause pseudoachondroplasia. Cyclical intravenous bisphosphonates reduce fracture rates in children.

Activating FGFR3 mutations inhibit chondrocyte proliferation in the physis. Most cases are new mutations, linked to older paternal age. Infants are at risk from foramen magnum stenosis and adults from lumbar spinal stenosis. DTDST mutations cause diastrophic dysplasia and SHOX deficiency causes Léri–Weill dyschondrosteosis.
A 2-year-old has bow legs. Which metaphyseal–diaphyseal (Drennan) angle most strongly suggests infantile Blount disease rather than physiological bowing?

An angle above about 16° strongly suggests Blount disease, while angles under about 10° are usually physiological, with an indeterminate zone between. Early walking and obesity are risk factors. Langenskiöld stages I–VI describe progression of the medial proximal tibial changes.
In normal development, physiological genu valgum is usually greatest at about:

Children are in varus at birth, straight at about 18–24 months and in maximum valgus at about 3–4 years, settling to adult valgus by about 7 years. Asymmetry, severe deformity or short stature warrant investigation.
Which Salter–Harris physeal injury is most often recognised only in retrospect, when growth arrest appears?

Type V is a crush injury of the physis with normal initial radiographs and the worst prognosis for growth. Type II, which exits through the metaphysis (Thurston Holland fragment), is the most common type.
Under the Ottawa ankle rules, an ankle radiograph is indicated after injury if there is pain in the malleolar zone and:
Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the distal 6 cm of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps

The rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures and reduce unnecessary radiographs. Foot radiographs are indicated for tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to bear weight. Swelling and bruising alone are not criteria.
After a twisting injury, a patient has medial ankle tenderness and swelling, no fracture on ankle radiographs, and tenderness over the proximal fibula. The most likely injury and key step are:
Maisonneuve injury; full-length tibia–fibula radiographs and assessment of syndesmotic stability

A Maisonneuve injury is a proximal fibular fracture with syndesmotic and deltoid (or medial malleolar) disruption. The unstable syndesmosis usually needs fixation with screws or a suture-button device. Always palpate the whole fibula after an ankle injury.
On an AP ankle radiograph, which measurement taken 1 cm above the plafond suggests a syndesmotic injury?
Tibiofibular clear space of more than 6 mm

A tibiofibular clear space over 6 mm, or reduced tibiofibular overlap, suggests diastasis. CT, stress views or intraoperative stress testing confirm it. A normal medial clear space is about 4 mm or less and equal to the superior clear space.
In an isolated Weber B fibular fracture, an external-rotation stress view shows the medial clear space widening to 6 mm. This indicates:
Deep deltoid ligament incompetence, making the ankle unstable
A stable injury suitable for a boot

A medial clear space over about 4–5 mm (or wider than the superior clear space) on stress views implies a deep deltoid injury, so the fracture is functionally bimalleolar and unstable. Weight-bearing radiographs are increasingly used: if the mortise stays congruent when weight-bearing, many are treated non-operatively.
An ankle fracture has a vertical medial malleolar fracture and a transverse fibular fracture below the syndesmosis. What must be looked for and addressed at surgery?
Impaction of the anteromedial tibial plafond

This is a supination–adduction injury: the talus drives medially, shearing off the medial malleolus and often impacting the adjacent plafond. The impacted segment should be elevated and grafted, and the vertical medial malleolus fixed with an antiglide plate or screws parallel to the joint.
In Hawkins' classification of talar neck fractures, type II is a displaced fracture with:
Dislocation of both subtalar and ankle joints
Subluxation or dislocation of the subtalar joint only
Dislocation of subtalar, ankle and talonavicular joints

Type I is undisplaced, type II adds subtalar dislocation, type III adds ankle dislocation, and type IV (Canale–Kelly) adds talonavicular dislocation. The risk of AVN rises with each type. Displaced fractures need urgent reduction and usually internal fixation.
A snowboarder has a 'sprained ankle' with tenderness just below the tip of the lateral malleolus, and radiographs are reported as normal. Which fracture is most often missed in this setting?

The lateral process fracture follows dorsiflexion with inversion and external rotation. It is subtle on mortise views and best seen on CT. Missed fragments lead to subtalar arthritis; large displaced fragments are fixed and small comminuted ones excised.
A tongue-type calcaneal fracture is displaced, and the skin over the posterior heel is tented and blanched. Best management:
Urgent reduction and fixation of the tuberosity fragment
Elevation and delayed fixation after 2 weeks
Below-knee cast in equinus for 6 weeks

The tuberosity fragment, pulled upwards by the Achilles tendon, can cause full-thickness posterior skin necrosis. This is a surgical emergency needing prompt percutaneous or open reduction and fixation, whereas most calcaneal fractures wait for swelling to settle.
The extensile lateral approach to the calcaneus depends on which vessel for the viability of its full-thickness flap?
Medial calcaneal branch of the posterior tibial artery

The vertical limb of the L-shaped incision lies anterior to the Achilles tendon but behind the lateral calcaneal artery, usually a branch of the peroneal artery, which supplies the flap's corner. Wound complications are common, so the sinus tarsi approach is often preferred.
On an AP foot radiograph, which alignment is normal and is lost in a Lisfranc injury?
Medial border of the 3rd metatarsal aligns with the medial border of the cuboid
Medial border of the 4th metatarsal aligns with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform
Medial border of the 2nd metatarsal aligns with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform
Lateral border of the 2nd metatarsal aligns with the lateral border of the medial cuneiform

The medial border of the 2nd metatarsal base should line up with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform on the AP view. On the oblique view, the medial border of the 4th metatarsal lines up with the medial border of the cuboid. Weight-bearing comparison views help detect subtle injuries.
A 25-year-old has a purely ligamentous, displaced Lisfranc injury. Compared with ORIF, primary partial arthrodesis of the medial TMT joints has been shown to give:
Higher rates of non-union and worse function
Gait impairment from loss of essential midfoot motion
Similar or better function with fewer secondary operations

Purely ligamentous injuries heal less reliably than bony ones, and ORIF often needs later hardware removal or salvage fusion. Randomised data support primary arthrodesis of the medial two or three TMT joints in this group; the medial column TMT joints have little essential motion. Bony injuries are generally fixed.

A 40-year-old felt a 'kick' behind the heel while playing badminton, and squeezing his calf with him prone produces no plantarflexion. For acute Achilles rupture, functional non-operative treatment with early protected weight-bearing, compared with surgery, gives:
Similar re-rupture rates with fewer wound complications
A much higher re-rupture rate, so it has been abandoned
No benefit at all in active patients

Randomised trials show that functional rehabilitation with early controlled motion gives re-rupture rates close to those after surgery while avoiding wound complications. Surgery is still considered for late presentation, a large gap or elite athletes. A positive Thompson (Simmonds) test confirms rupture.

A 55-year-old woman has medial ankle pain and a progressive flatfoot. She cannot do a single-leg heel rise, more toes are visible from behind on the affected side, and the hindfoot is flexible. Stage (Johnson and Strom) and typical surgery:
