In the Silfverskiöld test, flexing the knee relaxes gastrocnemius, which crosses the knee. Isolated gastrocnemius tightness is treated with stretching or gastrocnemius recession; if dorsiflexion stays limited with the knee flexed, soleus is also tight and Achilles lengthening may be needed.
In the AO Spine thoracolumbar injury classification, an injury with displacement of the cranial spine on the caudal spine in any plane is:

Type A injuries are compression injuries (A0 minor to A4 complete burst), type B are failures of the posterior or anterior tension band, and type C are translation or dislocation injuries, which are the most unstable. Neurological status and case-specific modifiers such as PLC injury and ankylosing disease are added.
Under the Subaxial Cervical Spine Injury Classification (SLIC), surgery is generally recommended when the total score is:

SLIC adds injury morphology, the discoligamentous complex and neurological status, with an extra point for continuing cord compression with a deficit. A score of 3 or less suggests non-operative treatment and 4 is indeterminate. It mirrors the TLICS system for the thoracolumbar spine.
After a high-energy injury, CT shows an avulsion fracture of the occipital condyle at the attachment of the alar ligament. In the Anderson–Montesano classification this is:
Type III, avulsion fracture, which may signal craniocervical instability
Type II, extension of a basilar skull fracture

Types I and II are usually stable and treated in a collar. Type III avulsions may accompany occipitocervical dissociation, so MRI and careful assessment of the craniocervical junction are needed; unstable injuries are treated with occipitocervical fusion.

An elderly woman has persistent back pain months after a minor osteoporotic vertebral fracture. Radiographs show progressive collapse with a horizontal gas-filled cleft within the vertebral body. This is:
Kümmell disease (osteonecrosis with an intravertebral vacuum cleft)

The vacuum cleft reflects avascular necrosis and non-union of the fracture, and the cleft may fill with fluid on MRI. The fracture is often mobile on flexion–extension or supine versus standing views. Vertebral augmentation can help, and fixation is needed for neurological compromise or kyphosis.
In the Genant semiquantitative method for osteoporotic vertebral fractures, a grade 2 (moderate) fracture has a vertebral height loss of about:

Grade 1 (mild) is 20–25% height loss, grade 2 (moderate) 25–40% and grade 3 (severe) more than 40%. A single prevalent vertebral fracture greatly increases the risk of further vertebral and hip fractures and is an indication for osteoporosis treatment.
A 50-year-old has thoracic myelopathy from a large, central, calcified T8–T9 disc herniation. Which approach should be avoided?

Removing a central thoracic disc through a laminectomy requires retracting the cord, which has a narrow canal and a tenuous blood supply in this region, and historically caused high rates of paralysis. Anterior (transthoracic or thoracoscopic) or posterolateral approaches that avoid cord retraction are used. Calcified discs may adhere to the dura.
On lumbar MRI of an adult, a low-lying conus medullaris suggesting a tethered cord is one that ends below about:

The conus normally ends at about L1–L2 in adults. A tethered cord, often with a thickened filum terminale (over about 2 mm) or lipoma, can cause back and leg pain, gait problems, foot deformity and bladder dysfunction, sometimes first appearing in adulthood. Symptomatic cases are treated by untethering.
A 15-year-old fast bowler has low back pain on extension. MRI shows bone oedema in the L5 pars without a complete fracture line. Initial management:
Stop the provoking sport, with activity modification, physiotherapy and possibly a brace

An early pars stress reaction can heal if load is removed, so stopping extension and rotation sports for about 3 months is the mainstay. MRI avoids radiation and shows oedema before a fracture line appears. Direct repair is considered for persistent symptoms with no slip and a healthy disc; fusion is for slips or failed repair.
A man has neck pain radiating to the middle finger, weak elbow extension and a reduced triceps reflex. The most likely level of disc prolapse is:

In the cervical spine each root exits above its own pedicle, so a C6–C7 disc compresses the C7 root, which is the most commonly affected. A C5–C6 disc affects C6 (biceps and brachioradialis, thumb), and C7–T1 affects C8 (finger flexors, little finger).
A patient with cervical radiculopathy finds that resting the hand on top of the head relieves the arm pain. This is the:

Shoulder abduction shortens the course of the root and reduces tension on it, so relief points to radicular rather than shoulder pathology. Spurling's test (extension, rotation and axial compression towards the painful side) reproduces radicular pain. Lhermitte and Hoffmann signs point to cord involvement.
A 65-year-old has multilevel cervical spondylotic myelopathy from C3 to C6. Which alignment favours posterior laminoplasty over anterior surgery?

Laminoplasty decompresses the cord by letting it drift backwards, which needs a lordotic or straight spine. In a kyphotic spine the cord stays draped over anterior compression, so anterior decompression, or posterior fusion that corrects alignment, is preferred. Instability also needs fusion rather than motion-preserving laminoplasty.

Years after apparently healed childhood spinal tuberculosis, a 30-year-old with a severe thoracic kyphosis develops slowly progressive paraparesis. MRI shows no active disease, with the cord stretched over a bony ridge at the apex. Compared with paraplegia during active disease, this late-onset paraplegia:
Has a better prognosis and needs only antitubercular drugs
Has a poorer prognosis and usually needs anterior decompression of the internal gibbus

Paraplegia during active disease is mainly from abscess, granulation tissue or sequestra and often responds to drugs and decompression. Late-onset paraplegia of healed disease is caused by the internal salient (gibbus) and fibrosis and recovers less well. Preventing severe kyphosis in children is therefore important.
In the Lenke classification of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, a minor curve is considered structural when its Cobb angle on side-bending radiographs remains:

Lenke combines curve type (1–6, by which regional curves are structural), a lumbar modifier (A–C, by the position of the lumbar apex relative to the CSVL) and a sagittal thoracic modifier. Thoracic kyphosis over 40° from T2 to T5 or T10 to L2 also makes a curve structural. Usually only structural curves are fused.
In a skeletally immature adolescent with idiopathic scoliosis of 20–40°, the BrAIST trial showed that bracing:
Has no effect on curve progression
Only works when worn for under 6 hours a day
Reduces progression to the surgical threshold, with more benefit the more hours it is worn

Rigid bracing significantly reduced progression to 50° or more compared with observation, with a dose–response relationship to hours of wear (about 13 hours a day or more giving high success). Bracing aims to stop progression, not to correct the curve.
After multilevel cervical laminectomy for an intramedullary tumour, a 7-year-old is at particular risk of:

Children have more elastic ligaments, horizontally oriented facets and growing vertebral bodies, so loss of the posterior tension band after laminectomy commonly leads to kyphosis and swan-neck deformity. Laminoplasty, preserving the facets, or fusion are used, with long-term radiographic follow-up.
A man with ankylosing spondylitis has a fixed chin-on-chest deformity and cannot see ahead. Corrective extension osteotomy is classically performed at C7–T1 because:
The spinal cord ends at this level
The vertebral arteries usually lie outside the transverse foramen of C7
The C8 root is not at risk
Fusion never occurs at this level

The vertebral arteries usually enter the transverse foramina at C6, so they are less at risk at C7–T1, the canal is relatively wide and the C8 root tolerates some stretch. The deformity is assessed with the chin–brow vertical angle, and correction aims to restore horizontal gaze without overcorrection.
In acute traumatic spinal cord injury, which haemodynamic target is commonly recommended for about the first week?
Mean arterial pressure of about 60 mmHg
Mean arterial pressure of about 85–90 mmHg or higher

Avoiding hypotension maintains cord perfusion and may improve neurological recovery, so guidelines recommend keeping the MAP at about 85–90 mmHg for about 5–7 days, often with vasopressors in a high-dependency setting. Hypotension in cervical injuries may come from neurogenic shock, but bleeding must be excluded first.
A long-distance runner has lateral knee pain that begins after a few kilometres. Pressure over the lateral femoral epicondyle with the knee flexed to about 30° reproduces the pain. Diagnosis:

Pain in Noble's test occurs as the iliotibial band passes over the lateral epicondyle at about 30° of flexion. The Ober test shows band tightness. Treatment is activity modification, stretching and hip abductor strengthening; surgical release is rarely needed.
A baseball pitcher has medial elbow pain and loss of velocity from a complete ulnar collateral ligament tear. In 'Tommy John' reconstruction, the graft most commonly used is the:

An ipsilateral palmaris longus autograft (or gracilis if absent) is passed through bone tunnels in the sublime tubercle and medial epicondyle to recreate the anterior bundle. The ulnar nerve is at risk and is often transposed if symptomatic. Most athletes return to their previous level after a long rehabilitation.
In a positive pivot shift test, the subluxed lateral tibial plateau reduces with a clunk at about 20–40° of flexion because:
The iliotibial band moves from in front of to behind the axis of knee flexion

In extension with valgus and internal rotation, the ACL-deficient tibia subluxes anterolaterally. As the knee flexes, the iliotibial band passes behind the flexion axis and pulls the tibia back. The test is highly specific for ACL deficiency, and a high-grade shift suggests additional anterolateral injury.
An anatomical posterolateral corner reconstruction (LaPrade technique) recreates which three structures?
Biceps femoris, iliotibial band and lateral meniscus
Fibular collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament
Arcuate ligament, fabellofibular ligament and lateral gastrocnemius

These three are the main static stabilisers of the posterolateral corner against varus and external rotation. Chronic grade III injuries usually need reconstruction rather than repair, and unaddressed PLC injury is a leading cause of ACL or PCL graft failure.
A patient with chronic posterolateral corner and cruciate insufficiency walks with a varus thrust and has genu varum. Which procedure should be considered first?

Varus alignment repeatedly stretches posterolateral reconstructions, so a valgus-producing osteotomy is often done first or together with reconstruction. Increasing the tibial slope with the osteotomy can also help PCL deficiency. Some patients become stable enough after osteotomy alone.
Which patient is the best candidate for meniscal allograft transplantation?
A 30-year-old with pain in a compartment after total meniscectomy, a stable knee and normal alignment
A 25-year-old with an intact meniscus and an ACL tear
An obese 50-year-old with varus deformity and bone-on-bone arthritis

Allograft transplantation aims to relieve symptoms after meniscectomy in young patients with preserved cartilage. Malalignment and instability must be corrected first or at the same time. Advanced arthritis and obesity are contraindications.
After microfracture of a full-thickness chondral defect, the defect fills mainly with:
Hyaline cartilage rich in type II collagen
Fibrocartilage rich in type I collagen

Microfracture recruits marrow-derived mesenchymal cells into a clot that matures into fibrocartilage, which is mechanically inferior and may deteriorate over time. It suits small lesions (generally under about 2–4 cm²). Larger lesions in young patients are often treated with autologous chondrocyte implantation or osteochondral grafting.
For a symptomatic 5 cm² full-thickness chondral defect of the femoral condyle in a 28-year-old with normal alignment and a stable knee, a commonly recommended procedure is:

MACI involves harvesting cartilage arthroscopically, culturing chondrocytes and implanting them on a scaffold at a second operation, producing hyaline-like tissue. It is used for larger defects in young patients. Osteochondral allograft is an alternative, especially when the subchondral bone is involved.
A dancer has an audible, painful clunk deep in the groin when bringing the hip from flexion, abduction and external rotation into extension. The likely cause is:
Iliotibial band snapping over the greater trochanter
Iliopsoas tendon snapping over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head

Internal snapping hip involves iliopsoas and can be shown on dynamic ultrasound. External snapping hip is the iliotibial band or gluteus maximus snapping over the greater trochanter, often visible laterally. Most cases settle with stretching; resistant cases may need tendon lengthening.
A 60-year-old diabetic man falls on stairs and cannot extend his knee. There is a palpable gap above the patella, which sits low on the lateral radiograph. Diagnosis:

Quadriceps tendon ruptures usually occur in people over 40, often with diabetes, renal disease, steroid use or gout, and the patella drops (patella baja). Patellar tendon ruptures occur in younger people and cause patella alta. Complete ruptures need early repair, as delay makes retraction difficult to overcome.
The most common location of acetabular labral tears is the:

The anterosuperior labrum is the zone most affected by FAI and dysplasia and is the least well vascularised. MR arthrography is more sensitive than standard MRI. Underlying bony morphology should be corrected when treating the labrum.
A rugby player has posterior shoulder pain. With the arm flexed to 90° and internally rotated, axial load applied while moving the arm across the body produces a painful clunk. This suggests:
Posterior instability with a posteroinferior labral tear

This is the jerk test, often paired with the Kim test (axial load with diagonal elevation). Posterior instability is common in linemen and lifters who load the arm in front of the body. Arthroscopic posterior labral repair and capsulorrhaphy is used when rehabilitation fails.
For a 50-year-old with an irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear and no glenohumeral arthritis, superior capsular reconstruction aims to:
Transfer latissimus dorsi to the subscapularis
Restore the superior restraint and keep the humeral head centred, improving the deltoid's function

A graft (fascia lata autograft or dermal allograft) is fixed from the superior glenoid to the greater tuberosity to resist superior translation of the head. Other options include partial repair, tendon transfers and balloon spacers; reverse arthroplasty is generally preferred in older patients or when arthritis is present.
A veteran baseball pitcher has posterior shoulder pain. CT shows a crescent-shaped exostosis at the posteroinferior glenoid rim. This is a:

A Bennett lesion is mineralisation of the posterior capsule origin from traction during the deceleration phase of throwing, often with posterior labral and undersurface cuff damage. Many are asymptomatic; symptomatic ones may be debrided arthroscopically. A Kim lesion is a concealed incomplete avulsion of the posteroinferior labrum.
An 11-year-old boy with wide-open physes and several years of growth left has a complete ACL tear and recurrent instability. The approach that best protects growth is:
Adult-type transphyseal reconstruction with a bone block across the physis
Physeal-sparing reconstruction (such as an iliotibial band technique or all-epiphyseal tunnels)
Wait until skeletal maturity with no restrictions
Primary repair with a screw across the physis

Delaying reconstruction in active children with instability leads to further meniscal and chondral damage. In prepubescent children, techniques that avoid the physes, or small central soft-tissue grafts without bone blocks or hardware across the physis, reduce the risk of growth arrest. Transphyseal techniques are used near maturity.
A 16-year-old has a first-time lateral patellar dislocation. Which finding is the clearest indication for early surgery?
A large osteochondral fragment or loose body

Most first-time dislocations are treated non-operatively, with bracing and quadriceps and hip strengthening. A displaced osteochondral fracture, often from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle, should be fixed or removed early, usually with MPFL repair or reconstruction at the same sitting.

A 60-year-old woman has pain under the second metatarsal head, and the second toe is drifting medially over the hallux. Vertical stress of the second MTP joint reproduces pain and shows dorsal translation. The structure torn is the:
Plantar plate of the second MTP joint

The modified Lachman or drawer test of the MTP joint shows plantar plate insufficiency, which leads to crossover toe deformity. A long second metatarsal and hallux valgus are risk factors. Treatment ranges from taping and stiff-soled shoes to plantar plate repair with a Weil osteotomy.

A runner has numbness on the dorsum of the foot and pain over the lower lateral leg, worse with exercise. Tinel's sign is positive about 10–12 cm above the tip of the lateral malleolus. The nerve affected is the:

The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the deep fascia of the lateral compartment in the distal leg, where it can be entrapped, especially after ankle sprains or with a fascial defect. Treatment is fascial release at the exit point if conservative measures fail. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the first web space.

A 13-year-old girl has a painful prominence over the medial midfoot. Radiographs show a large accessory navicular joined to the navicular by a synchondrosis. If non-operative treatment fails, the usual procedure is:
Excision of the accessory bone with reattachment or advancement of the tibialis posterior tendon (Kidner procedure)

Type II accessory naviculars, joined by a synchondrosis, are most often symptomatic as the tibialis posterior tendon pulls on the fibrocartilaginous junction. Excising the ossicle and securing the tendon to the navicular relieves pain. Type I is a sesamoid in the tendon and type III a fused cornuate navicular.
A 45-year-old has a painless firm nodule in the medial arch of the plantar fascia. Biopsy is consistent with plantar fibromatosis. Appropriate initial management:

Ledderhose disease is a fibroproliferative disorder similar to Dupuytren disease. Local excision has high recurrence rates and can leave painful scars, so most patients are managed with offloading insoles. Total plantar fasciectomy is reserved for aggressive, symptomatic disease, and radiotherapy is used in some centres.
When creating the anterolateral portal for ankle arthroscopy, the structure most at risk is the:
Deep peroneal nerve and dorsalis pedis artery

The anterolateral portal is placed lateral to peroneus tertius, close to branches of the superficial peroneal nerve, which can often be seen or felt with the foot in plantarflexion and inversion. Nerve injury is the most common complication of ankle arthroscopy. The anteromedial portal, medial to tibialis anterior, risks the saphenous nerve and vein.
In the cavovarus foot of Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, the plantarflexed first ray results from:
A strong peroneus longus overpowering a weak tibialis anterior
A strong tibialis anterior overpowering a weak peroneus longus

Weak tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis are opposed by stronger peroneus longus and tibialis posterior, giving a plantarflexed first ray and hindfoot varus. Surgery balances tendons (such as transferring peroneus longus to brevis) and corrects bony deformity. Testing the hindfoot with the Coleman block guides the procedure.
On a weight-bearing lateral radiograph of a cavus foot, the line along the talus and the line along the first metatarsal (Meary's angle) meet with the apex pointing:

In the normal foot these lines are roughly collinear. In cavus the first metatarsal is plantarflexed, so the lines meet at an apex-dorsal angle; in planus the talus is plantarflexed, so the apex points plantarwards. Calcaneal pitch is also increased in cavus.
A woman with rheumatoid arthritis has severe hallux valgus, dislocated lesser MTP joints and painful plantar callosities. A commonly recommended reconstruction is:
Keller resection with lesser toe tenotomies only
First MTP arthrodesis with resection of the lesser metatarsal heads

First MTP fusion gives a stable medial column and lower recurrence than resection arthroplasty, and lesser metatarsal head resection relieves the plantar pressure from the dislocated joints. Joint-preserving osteotomies are increasingly used in patients whose disease is well controlled with modern drugs.
A diabetic patient has a recurrent ulcer under the first metatarsal head and an equinus contracture. Which procedure most reduces forefoot plantar pressure and recurrence?

Equinus increases forefoot loading during gait. Achilles lengthening combined with total contact casting heals more forefoot ulcers and reduces recurrence than casting alone, although overlengthening can cause heel ulcers.
Which is a contraindication to total ankle arthroplasty?

Neuropathic joints, active infection, a non-viable talus from extensive osteonecrosis, severe uncorrectable deformity and poor soft tissues are contraindications. Arthrodesis remains the standard alternative. Older, lower-demand patients with good bone stock and alignment are ideal candidates.
The most common cause of end-stage ankle arthritis is:

Unlike the hip and knee, most ankle arthritis is post-traumatic, following malleolar or pilon fractures or chronic lateral ankle instability, so patients tend to be younger. Primary osteoarthritis of the ankle is relatively uncommon, possibly because of the thick, congruent cartilage.
In an ankle fracture with a large posterior malleolar fragment and a syndesmotic injury, fixation of the posterior malleolus often restores syndesmotic stability because:
The deltoid ligament attaches to it
It contains the tibialis posterior groove
The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament attaches to the posterior malleolar fragment
The anterior tibiofibular ligament attaches to it

The PITFL is the strongest part of the syndesmosis and usually stays attached to the posterior malleolar fragment, so reducing and fixing the fragment restores much of syndesmotic stability and the incisura. CT helps define fragment size and pattern (such as Haraguchi types).

A footballer has anterior ankle pain on dorsiflexion with tenderness along the anterior joint line. A lateral radiograph shows osteophytes on the anterior tibia and talar neck. If conservative measures fail, treatment is:

Anterior bony impingement ('footballer's ankle') results from repeated forced dorsiflexion and capsular traction. Arthroscopic debridement gives good results when the joint space is preserved. Anterolateral soft-tissue impingement after sprains shows no bony spurs.

A military recruit has diffuse heel pain after a long march. Squeezing the heel from both sides reproduces the pain, and radiographs at 3 weeks show a sclerotic band across the posterior calcaneus. Diagnosis:

The calcaneal squeeze test is positive, and the fracture line is usually perpendicular to the trabeculae of the posterior tuberosity. Early radiographs are often normal, so MRI confirms it sooner. Treatment is protected weight-bearing in a boot for several weeks.

In an adolescent with hallux valgus, which radiographic finding means a distal metatarsal osteotomy with soft-tissue release alone may leave an incongruent joint, so the articular angle must also be corrected?

The DMAA describes how the articular surface of the first metatarsal head is tilted relative to the metatarsal axis; normally under about 10°. A high DMAA with a congruent joint is common in juvenile hallux valgus and needs an osteotomy that rotates the articular surface, as lateral release would make the joint incongruent.
A runner has chronic medial heel pain that radiates laterally and some weakness of little toe abduction. Plantar fasciitis treatment has failed. The nerve likely entrapped is the:
First branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter's nerve)

Baxter's nerve runs between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae and supplies abductor digiti minimi; long-standing entrapment can cause fatty atrophy of that muscle on MRI. It commonly coexists with plantar fasciitis. Release of the nerve with partial plantar fascia release is used for resistant cases.

A 65-year-old has foot slap and difficulty clearing the toes after stumbling. There is a painless swelling on the front of the ankle, weak ankle dorsiflexion with toe extensors substituting, and normal sensation. Diagnosis:

Tibialis anterior ruptures typically occur in older people, often with minimal trauma, and are often missed. Sensation is normal and the extensor hallucis and digitorum longus contract to compensate. Active patients usually benefit from repair or reconstruction; low-demand patients may manage with an ankle–foot orthosis.
Osteoclasts seal onto the bone surface to form the resorption compartment mainly through which integrin?

The sealing zone isolates a space under the ruffled border, into which the osteoclast pumps hydrogen ions (generated by carbonic anhydrase II) and secretes cathepsin K to dissolve mineral and digest collagen, forming a Howship lacuna. αIIbβ3 is the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor.
Which of these markers reflects bone resorption rather than bone formation?
C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX)

CTX and NTX are crosslinked collagen fragments released when osteoclasts degrade type I collagen. P1NP, bone-specific ALP and osteocalcin are products of osteoblasts and reflect formation. CTX has a marked diurnal rhythm, so it is measured on a fasting morning sample, and it falls quickly with antiresorptive treatment.
In articular cartilage, aggrecan molecules attach to a hyaluronan backbone and the attachment is stabilised by:

Aggrecan's core protein carries chondroitin sulphate and keratan sulphate chains whose fixed negative charges draw in water, giving cartilage its compressive stiffness. Decorin is a small proteoglycan that binds collagen fibrils, and lubricin provides boundary lubrication at the surface.
The enzyme mainly responsible for cleaving type II collagen in osteoarthritic cartilage is:

MMP-13 is the principal collagenase acting on type II collagen, while ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5 are aggrecanases that degrade aggrecan. Their expression is driven by IL-1 and TNF-α and opposed by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). Cathepsin K is the osteoclast's collagen-degrading enzyme.
Hyaluronic acid in synovial fluid is produced mainly by:

The synovial lining has no basement membrane. Type A cells are phagocytic, while type B cells secrete hyaluronic acid and lubricin. Synovial fluid is a plasma dialysate whose hyaluronic acid makes it viscous and shear-thinning: its viscosity falls as the rate of shear rises.
Adult articular chondrocytes receive their nutrition mainly by:
Diffusion from the synovial fluid, aided by cyclical loading
Capillaries crossing the tidemark from subchondral bone
Perichondrial vessels at the joint margin
Vessels running through the deep zone

Adult articular cartilage is avascular, aneural and alymphatic, so chondrocytes depend on diffusion, which joint loading and unloading helps to pump. This limited supply, along with sparse cells trapped in matrix, explains why partial-thickness defects do not heal.
Which type of muscle contraction generates the greatest force and is most associated with muscle strain and delayed-onset muscle soreness?

In eccentric contraction the muscle lengthens while it contracts, as in the hamstrings decelerating the leg at the end of swing. It produces the highest force for the least energy and causes most strains and delayed-onset soreness. Concentric contraction shortens the muscle, isometric keeps its length constant, and isokinetic keeps joint velocity constant.
Acute indirect muscle strains most commonly occur at the:

The myotendinous junction is the weakest link in an otherwise healthy muscle–tendon unit. Strains are most common in muscles that cross two joints and have a high proportion of type II fibres, such as the hamstrings, rectus femoris and medial gastrocnemius, usually during eccentric contraction.
After primary repair of a flexor tendon, the repair is at its weakest at about:

During the inflammatory phase the tendon ends soften and the repair relies almost entirely on the suture. Strength then rises as collagen is laid down in the proliferative phase and remodelled. Early controlled motion improves tendon gliding and repair strength compared with complete immobilisation.
Investigators compare infection rates (infected or not infected) between two independent groups of patients. The appropriate statistical test is:
Chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test when expected counts are small

Comparing proportions of a categorical outcome between groups uses the chi-square test, with Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts are under about 5. The t-test compares means of continuous, normally distributed data (paired for repeated measures in the same patients), the Mann–Whitney U test is its non-parametric equivalent, and ANOVA compares means of three or more groups.
A case–control study of a rare tumour asks patients and controls to remember past exposures. Its main weakness is:

Cases tend to search their memories harder for possible causes than controls do. Case–control studies are efficient for rare diseases and yield odds ratios. Cohort studies measure incidence and relative risk but suffer loss to follow-up, and lead-time bias affects evaluation of screening.
In a randomised trial, analysing patients in the groups to which they were randomised, whatever treatment they actually received (intention-to-treat analysis), mainly serves to:
Preserve the balance of known and unknown confounders created by randomisation

Intention-to-treat keeps the groups comparable and reflects real-world effectiveness, although crossover makes it conservative. A per-protocol analysis includes only patients who received the allocated treatment and may overestimate the effect, because those who deviate often differ systematically.
A material that fails with little or no plastic deformation once its elastic limit is exceeded is described as:

Brittle materials such as ceramics, PMMA and glass have a stress–strain curve that ends abruptly near the yield point. Ductile materials, such as stainless steel, deform plastically before failing. Ceramics are hard and wear-resistant but have low fracture toughness.
The endurance limit of an implant material is the:
Maximum stress it withstands in a single load to failure
Strain at which it begins to deform plastically
Stress below which it can be loaded cyclically an effectively unlimited number of times without fatigue failure

Implants usually fail by fatigue from repeated loads well below their ultimate strength. If a fracture does not unite, fixation is in a race between healing and fatigue failure. Stress risers such as screw holes and surface scratches reduce fatigue life.
Compared with a closed-section intramedullary nail of the same diameter and material, a slotted (open-section) nail has:

A longitudinal slot greatly reduces the polar moment of inertia, so torsional rigidity falls markedly while bending stiffness is less affected. Nail stiffness rises roughly with the fourth power of its radius, so small increases in diameter have large effects.
Which single change most increases the stiffness of a unilateral external fixator?
Increasing the distance between the bone and the rod
Placing the pins in each fragment closer together

Pin bending stiffness rises with the fourth power of its radius. Stiffness also increases with more pins, wider pin spread within each fragment (one near and one far from the fracture), the rod closer to the bone, a second rod, and a second plane. Pin diameter should stay under about a third of the bone diameter to avoid fracture.
Parathyroid hormone stimulates bone resorption mainly by binding to receptors on:
Osteoblasts and osteocytes, which then increase RANKL and reduce OPG

Osteoclasts lack PTH receptors, so PTH acts through cells of the osteoblast lineage, which signal to osteoclast precursors. Calcitonin, by contrast, acts directly on osteoclast receptors. Continuous PTH excess is catabolic, while intermittent PTH analogues such as teriparatide are anabolic.
In the modified Gartland classification of extension-type supracondylar humerus fractures, type II is:
Displaced but with the posterior cortex intact as a hinge
Completely displaced with no cortical contact
Unstable in both flexion and extension

Type I is undisplaced, type II angulated with an intact posterior hinge, type III completely displaced, and type IV unstable in flexion and extension, usually recognised under anaesthesia. Type II fractures in which the anterior humeral line misses the capitellum are usually treated with closed reduction and pinning.
On a true lateral elbow radiograph of a school-age child, the anterior humeral line normally passes through the:

In an extension-type supracondylar fracture the capitellum moves backwards, so the line passes through its anterior third or misses it entirely. In very young children the line can normally pass through the anterior third. A raised posterior fat pad indicates an effusion and possibly an occult fracture.
The most common long-term complication of a supracondylar humerus fracture in children is:

Cubitus varus results from medial collapse or rotational malreduction and does not remodel. It is mainly cosmetic but has been linked to later lateral condyle fracture, posterolateral instability and ulnar neuropathy. It is corrected with a lateral closing-wedge osteotomy; Baumann's angle helps judge coronal alignment at reduction.
In the usual sequence of appearance of the elbow ossification centres, the last to appear is the:

The order is captured by CRITOE: capitellum, radial head, internal (medial) epicondyle, trochlea, olecranon and external (lateral) epicondyle. If the trochlea is ossified but the medial epicondyle is not in its usual place, suspect that the epicondyle has been avulsed and trapped in the joint.
A 7-year-old has greenstick fractures of both forearm bones with apex-volar angulation. This pattern usually results from a supination force, so it is reduced by:

Rotational mechanisms explain greenstick fractures: apex-volar fractures come from supination and are reduced by pronation, while apex-dorsal fractures come from pronation and are reduced by supination. Remodelling is greatest close to the physis and in the plane of joint motion, but rotational deformity does not remodel.
In a child with a forearm fracture, which line must be checked on every elbow view so that a Monteggia injury is not missed?
Radiocapitellar line (the axis of the radial neck passing through the capitellum)

A line along the radial neck should pass through the centre of the capitellum in all projections. A missed radial head dislocation becomes a chronic Monteggia lesion with pain, restricted motion and later valgus or instability, and reconstruction with an ulnar osteotomy is far more difficult than early reduction.
In a 9-year-old with a radial neck fracture, closed treatment is generally acceptable when angulation is less than about:

Children remodel radial neck angulation well up to about 30°. Greater angulation, or a block to rotation, is treated by closed manipulation or percutaneous or intramedullary (Metaizeau) reduction. Open reduction is a last resort because it risks avascular necrosis, stiffness and posterior interosseous nerve injury.
In a neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy, which finding by about 3 months of age is classically used to predict good spontaneous recovery?

Upper plexus (C5–C6, Erb) palsies with early biceps recovery usually do well. Absent biceps recovery by about 3–6 months is a common indication for microsurgical reconstruction. Horner syndrome and a flail limb suggest lower root avulsion and a poor prognosis. Internal rotation contracture and glenohumeral dysplasia are common late problems.

An infant has congenital muscular torticollis with a palpable sternocleidomastoid 'tumour'; the head tilts towards the affected side and the chin rotates away. Which condition should be specifically screened for?

Torticollis is considered a 'packaging' problem linked with intrauterine crowding, as are DDH and metatarsus adductus, so the hips should be examined and imaged as needed. Most cases resolve with stretching; release of the sternocleidomastoid is considered if it persists beyond about 1 year. Ocular and cervical spine causes should be excluded when there is no tight muscle.
A child has a small, high-riding scapula with limited shoulder abduction. Radiographs show a bony bar running from the superomedial scapula to the cervical spine. The bar is the:

This is Sprengel deformity, a failure of normal scapular descent, often associated with Klippel–Feil syndrome, scoliosis and renal anomalies. Significant cases are treated in early childhood with excision of the omovertebral bone and scapular repositioning, such as the Woodward procedure, taking care to avoid brachial plexus traction.
A 2-year-old has a painless, mobile lump over the middle of the right clavicle, present since infancy, with no history of trauma. Most likely diagnosis:

Congenital pseudarthrosis of the clavicle is almost always right-sided (left-sided only with dextrocardia), painless and without callus. A birth fracture heals quickly with abundant callus. Cleidocranial dysplasia gives bilateral hypoplasia or absence of the clavicles. Symptomatic or unsightly cases are treated with excision of the pseudarthrosis, grafting and fixation.
A 12-year-old basketball player has pain and tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella, and radiographs show fragmentation there. Diagnosis:

Sinding-Larsen–Johansson syndrome is a traction apophysitis at the origin of the patellar tendon and settles with activity modification. Osgood–Schlatter affects the tibial tubercle. A sleeve fracture is an acute avulsion of a cartilage sleeve with loss of active extension and needs fixation, and a bipartite patella is usually superolateral.
A 6-year-old has bilateral, symmetrical and simultaneous irregularity and flattening of both femoral capital epiphyses. Before diagnosing Perthes disease, the most important next step is to:
Obtain a skeletal survey and thyroid function tests to look for an epiphyseal dysplasia or hypothyroidism

Perthes disease is bilateral in a minority of children, and then the hips are usually at different stages. Symmetrical, simultaneous changes suggest multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia or hypothyroidism; sickle cell disease and Gaucher disease are other causes of bilateral osteonecrosis.
In Herring's prospective multicentre study of Perthes disease, which group did better with surgical containment (femoral or innominate osteotomy) than with non-operative treatment?
All children under 6 years at onset
Children over 8 years at onset with lateral pillar B or B/C border hips
Children with lateral pillar A hips at any age
Children with lateral pillar C hips at any age

Children under about 6 years at onset generally did well whatever the treatment, and lateral pillar A hips did well while pillar C hips did poorly regardless. The benefit of surgery was seen in older children with intermediate (B and B/C) involvement.
In SCFE, the Southwick slip angle (measured on the frog-lateral view relative to the normal side) classifies a severe slip as greater than:

Mild slips are under 30°, moderate 30–50° and severe over 50°. Severe slips leave a deformity that causes femoroacetabular impingement, and some centres perform subcapital realignment (modified Dunn procedure) through a surgical dislocation, which carries a risk of AVN.
Compared with a stable SCFE, an unstable SCFE (the child cannot walk, even with crutches) carries:
A much higher risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head
No risk of a contralateral slip
A lower risk of AVN because the physis is mobile

In Loder's series, AVN occurred in a large proportion of unstable slips but almost none of the stable ones. Unstable slips are fixed promptly, avoiding forceful manipulation. Chondrolysis is linked to screw penetration of the joint, and contralateral slips are common in both types.
A 9-month-old has a dislocated hip from DDH that has not been treated. Usual treatment:
Closed reduction under anaesthesia with arthrography, adductor tenotomy if needed and a hip spica in the human position
Open reduction with Salter osteotomy and femoral shortening

The Pavlik harness is much less successful after about 6 months of age. Closed reduction must be stable within Ramsey's safe zone, and reduction is confirmed with MRI or CT after spica application. Open reduction is used if closed reduction fails or is unstable, and pelvic and femoral osteotomies are usually added in older children.
In chronic osteomyelitis, the involucrum is:
Dead bone separated from living bone
A layer of new periosteal bone formed around the dead bone
A sinus tract to the skin
The granulation tissue lining an abscess

The sequestrum is the dead bone, and openings in the involucrum through which pus escapes are called cloacae. In children, the involucrum should be strong enough before sequestrectomy, otherwise removing the sequestrum can leave an unstable segmental defect or fracture.
A child with sickle cell disease has a painful, swollen leg with fever. Compared with osteomyelitis, bone infarction in sickle cell disease is:
Far more common, so the two must be distinguished carefully

Vaso-occlusive infarction is much more frequent than infection, and both cause pain, swelling and fever. Persistent high fever, raised and rising CRP, positive blood cultures and a fluid collection favour infection, and aspiration or biopsy settles doubt. Salmonella and S. aureus are the main organisms.
Which property must an antibiotic have to be mixed into PMMA bone cement for local delivery?
Heat stability during the exothermic polymerisation, and availability as a water-soluble powder

Gentamicin, tobramycin and vancomycin are commonly used. Elution is highest in the first days and depends on surface area and porosity, so beads release more than a solid spacer. Liquid antibiotics and very high doses weaken the cement, which matters for definitive fixation but less for temporary spacers.
Apart from Staphylococcus aureus, which organisms are typical causes of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis in neonates?
Group B streptococcus and Gram-negative enteric bacilli

Neonates may show few systemic signs and often have multifocal disease. Until about 18 months of age, vessels cross the physis, so metaphyseal infection can spread into the epiphysis and joint and cause growth disturbance. Kingella is typical of older toddlers.

A 10-year-old from an endemic area has a large, relatively painless knee effusion weeks after a tick bite and an expanding ring-shaped rash. Synovial white cell count is about 30,000 cells/µL. First-line treatment:
Oral doxycycline or amoxicillin for about 4 weeks

Lyme arthritis, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, typically causes a large effusion that is less painful than septic arthritis, and the diagnosis is confirmed serologically. A minority develop antibiotic-refractory arthritis that is treated with anti-inflammatory measures or synovectomy.
Two weeks after an episode of diarrhoea, a young man develops asymmetric arthritis of the knee and ankle, heel enthesitis and conjunctivitis. Synovial fluid is sterile. Most likely diagnosis:

Reactive arthritis follows enteric infection (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) or genitourinary infection (Chlamydia) and is associated with HLA-B27. The joint is sterile, and NSAIDs are the mainstay. It belongs to the spondyloarthropathies, along with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis.
A patient starting isoniazid for osteoarticular tuberculosis should also receive pyridoxine to prevent:

Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, pyrazinamide hyperuricaemia and hepatotoxicity, and rifampicin orange body fluids and liver enzyme induction. Treatment uses an intensive phase of four drugs followed by a continuation phase, and osteoarticular TB is commonly treated for longer than pulmonary TB.
In leprosy, which peripheral nerve is most commonly thickened and damaged?
Radial nerve in the spiral groove

Mycobacterium leprae prefers cooler, superficial nerve segments: the ulnar nerve at the elbow, median nerve at the wrist, common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck, posterior tibial nerve and great auricular nerve. This leads to claw hand, foot drop and insensate ulcers. Tendon transfers are performed once the disease is controlled.
A farmer who has never been immunised against tetanus has a deep, soil-contaminated wound of the leg. Tetanus prevention requires:
Thorough wound debridement, tetanus immunoglobulin and a full course of tetanus vaccine

Immunoglobulin gives immediate passive protection, while the vaccine, given at a different site, builds long-term immunity. Debridement removes the anaerobic environment that Clostridium tetani needs. Fully immunised patients with a tetanus-prone wound usually need only a booster if their last dose was long ago.
In suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis, the reference standard for diagnosis and for guiding antibiotic choice is:
Bone biopsy for culture and histology

Superficial swabs grow colonising organisms and correlate poorly with bone cultures. A positive probe-to-bone test is useful in a high-risk ulcer, and MRI is the best imaging test. Biopsy taken through intact skin or at surgery, ideally after a short antibiotic-free interval, identifies the true pathogen.
Plain radiographic signs of acute osteomyelitis, such as periosteal reaction and lytic destruction, usually appear only after about:

Bone must lose a substantial proportion of its mineral before destruction is visible. Deep soft-tissue swelling with loss of fat planes may be seen earlier. MRI is the imaging investigation of choice for early diagnosis and for detecting abscesses.
On a three-phase technetium bone scan, which pattern favours osteomyelitis over cellulitis?
Increased uptake in the flow and blood-pool phases only, with a normal delayed phase
Focal increased uptake in all three phases, including the delayed (bone) phase
Reduced uptake in all three phases
Normal flow with increased blood-pool activity only

Cellulitis causes diffuse increased activity in the early phases with little focal bone uptake on delayed images. A 'cold' scan can occur early in infection when intraosseous pressure is high, or with infarction. Specificity is poor after surgery, fracture or Charcot arthropathy, so MRI is usually preferred.
A plumber has a red, hot, fluctuant swelling over the olecranon with a small overlying abrasion; elbow movement is nearly full. The most likely organism is:

Septic bursitis of the olecranon and prepatellar bursae usually follows skin trauma and is mostly caused by S. aureus. Preserved elbow motion distinguishes it from septic arthritis. Aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals guides treatment, with antibiotics and bursectomy if it fails to settle.
A patient on long-term dialysis has a lateral spine radiograph showing ill-defined sclerotic bands along the vertebral end plates with lucent centres ('rugger-jersey spine'). This is typical of:

Chronic kidney disease causes phosphate retention, low calcitriol and raised PTH, producing a mix of hyperparathyroid bone disease and osteomalacia. Osteopetrosis produces sharply defined 'sandwich' vertebrae, and Paget's disease a 'picture-frame' vertebra.

An adult has bone pain, proximal muscle weakness and multiple insufficiency fractures. Serum phosphate is low with high urinary phosphate loss, FGF23 is raised and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low. There is no family history. The likely cause is:
Tumour-induced osteomalacia from a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour

These small, usually benign tumours, often in bone or soft tissue of the limbs, secrete FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting and suppressed calcitriol. They are localised with somatostatin-receptor imaging such as gallium-68 DOTATATE PET, and complete excision is curative.
A child has short stature, a round face, short fourth and fifth metacarpals and subcutaneous calcification. Serum calcium is low and phosphate high despite a raised PTH. Diagnosis:

End-organ resistance to PTH results from loss-of-function GNAS mutations, inherited from the mother. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism has the same physical features with normal biochemistry (paternal inheritance). In primary hypoparathyroidism PTH is low, and Turner syndrome can cause a short fourth metacarpal but with normal calcium.
Which bone graft substitute is resorbed most rapidly?

Calcium sulphate resorbs within weeks to a few months, sometimes faster than new bone forms, and can produce sterile wound drainage. β-tricalcium phosphate resorbs more slowly, and crystalline hydroxyapatite persists for years. All are osteoconductive only, unless combined with cells or growth factors.
Compared with fresh-frozen bone allograft, freeze-dried (lyophilised) allograft is:
Associated with a higher risk of viral transmission
Less immunogenic but mechanically weaker and more brittle

Freeze-drying reduces antigenicity but weakens the graft, particularly in torsion and bending, and it must be rehydrated before use. Fresh allograft is the most immunogenic and is used mainly for osteochondral transplantation. With modern donor screening, viral transmission is very rare.
The zone of Ranvier at the periphery of the physis is responsible for:
Growth of the physis in width (latitudinal growth)

The zone of Ranvier is a wedge-shaped group of progenitor cells at the edge of the physis, surrounded by the fibrous perichondrial ring of LaCroix, which gives mechanical support. Injury to this zone, as from burns, lawnmower injuries or deep abrasion, can form a peripheral physeal bar and angular deformity.
Which bone is the first to begin ossifying in the fetus and forms mainly by intramembranous ossification?

The clavicle ossifies largely in membrane, like the flat bones of the skull, while long bones form by endochondral ossification. Its medial physis is the last in the body to fuse, in the mid-twenties. Cleidocranial dysplasia (RUNX2) affects membranous bone, causing hypoplastic clavicles and delayed closure of the fontanelles.
Growth arrest after a physeal injury is most likely when which blood supply is damaged?
Epiphyseal vessels supplying the reserve and proliferative zones

Loss of the epiphyseal supply kills the germinal cells, so growth stops. Loss of the metaphyseal supply only interrupts calcification of the hypertrophic zone, which widens temporarily and then recovers. The proximal femoral epiphysis is almost entirely intra-articular, so its blood supply is particularly vulnerable.
In elective limb surgery, the generally accepted upper limit for continuous arterial tourniquet inflation before it is released is about:

Longer times increase the risk of muscle injury, post-tourniquet syndrome and nerve damage, which occurs mainly from pressure under the cuff edge; the radial nerve is most often affected in the upper limb. Pressure should be set relative to limb occlusion pressure, and wider cuffs occlude at lower pressures.
A surgeon moves from 0.5 m to 1 m away from the source of scattered radiation during fluoroscopy. Their exposure falls to about:

By the inverse square law, doubling the distance reduces exposure to a quarter. Other measures include standing on the image intensifier side (scatter is greatest on the tube side), keeping the tube under the table, using pulsed and low-dose modes, collimating, and wearing a lead apron and thyroid shield.
Which MRI sequence is most sensitive for detecting bone marrow oedema?
Short tau inversion recovery (STIR) or fat-suppressed T2

Fat suppression makes water bright against dark marrow fat, so oedema from contusion, stress injury, infection or tumour stands out. T1 images show anatomy and marrow replacement, which appears dark. Gradient-echo images show blooming of haemosiderin and metal.
Rivaroxaban, used for thromboprophylaxis after hip and knee arthroplasty, works by:
Enhancing antithrombin, which inhibits factor Xa and thrombin

Rivaroxaban and apixaban are oral direct factor Xa inhibitors that do not need routine monitoring. Low-molecular-weight heparin acts through antithrombin, dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, and warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing factors II, VII, IX and X.

During general anaesthesia for scoliosis surgery in a child with central core myopathy, end-tidal CO2 rises steeply with tachycardia, masseter and limb rigidity, and then hyperthermia. The specific treatment is:

This is malignant hyperthermia, usually from RYR1 mutations, triggered by volatile agents and suxamethonium. Stop the triggers, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, cool the patient, treat hyperkalaemia and give dantrolene. Boys with Duchenne dystrophy given these agents are at risk of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic arrest rather than true malignant hyperthermia.

Shortly after a large-volume bupivacaine regional block, a patient develops perioral tingling, then seizures and a ventricular arrhythmia. Besides airway support and seizure control, the specific treatment is:

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is treated with lipid emulsion, which acts as a sink for the lipid-soluble drug, along with standard resuscitation; cardiac arrest may need prolonged CPR. Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic of the common agents. Prevention relies on weight-based dosing, aspiration before injection and ultrasound guidance.
The metal most commonly responsible for cutaneous hypersensitivity in patients with orthopaedic implants is:

Nickel is the commonest metal allergen and is present in stainless steel; cobalt and chromium are next. Titanium allergy is rare. The role of metal hypersensitivity in implant pain or failure is uncertain, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection and mechanical causes.
A diagnostic test with fixed sensitivity and specificity is applied to a population in which the disease is much less common. Its positive predictive value will:

As prevalence falls, false positives make up a larger share of positive results, so PPV falls while NPV rises. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself and do not change with prevalence, which is why screening tests perform less well in low-risk populations.
Experimental studies of fracture healing show that cyclo-oxygenase-2 (COX-2) activity is:
Needed for normal differentiation of mesenchymal cells into osteoblasts and callus formation

Prostaglandins produced by COX-2 in the early inflammatory phase help drive osteogenic differentiation, and COX-2-deficient mice show impaired healing. The same mechanism explains why NSAIDs such as indomethacin prevent heterotopic ossification. The clinical effect of short NSAID courses on fracture healing remains debated.
In secondary (indirect) fracture healing, the soft callus consists mainly of:

The haematoma and inflammatory phase are followed by soft callus formed by chondrocytes and fibroblasts, which is then mineralised and replaced by woven bone through endochondral ossification (hard callus). Woven bone is remodelled into lamellar bone over months to years.
In a Seddon neurapraxia, nerve conduction studies typically show:
Absent responses to stimulation distal to the lesion after about 10 days
Reduced distal amplitude from Wallerian degeneration
A conduction block across the lesion with normal conduction in the segment distal to it

Neurapraxia is focal demyelination with intact axons, so there is no Wallerian degeneration and the distal nerve stays excitable; recovery is usually complete within weeks to months. In axonotmesis and neurotmesis the distal segment degenerates and becomes inexcitable after about 7–10 days.
By weight, the mineral (inorganic) phase of bone makes up about:

The mineral is mainly calcium hydroxyapatite. The organic matrix is about a quarter to a third of bone weight, of which roughly 90% is type I collagen, and water makes up the rest. Collagen gives bone tensile strength and the mineral gives compressive strength.
A healthy 2-year-old is brought in because of in-toeing. The thigh–foot angle is markedly internal and hip rotation is normal. Most likely cause and management:
Internal tibial torsion; reassurance, as most resolve spontaneously

In-toeing is typically due to metatarsus adductus in infants, internal tibial torsion in toddlers and femoral anteversion in children aged about 3–8, who sit in a 'W' position and have increased internal hip rotation. Shoes, braces and night splints do not change the natural history, and osteotomy is reserved for severe, persistent deformity in older children.
An infant has a bean-shaped foot with the forefoot adducted and a normal hindfoot. The heel bisector line passes through the third toe and the forefoot corrects passively past neutral. Management:
Observation and stretching, as most resolve

The heel bisector normally passes through the second toe; through the third toe is mild, the fourth moderate and the fifth severe (Bleck). Flexible metatarsus adductus resolves in most infants. Rigid deformities may be treated with serial casting in the first year. The normal hindfoot distinguishes it from clubfoot and skewfoot.
In a child with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, isolated Achilles tendon lengthening without addressing other levels commonly leads to:

Weakening the soleus breaks the plantarflexion–knee extension couple, so the knee and hip collapse into flexion. Modern practice uses gait analysis and single-event multilevel surgery to correct all levels together. Excessive hamstring lengthening, by contrast, can cause knee recurvatum.
In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, spinal fusion for scoliosis is generally advised:
Early, once a progressive curve develops, while pulmonary function is still adequate
Only in boys who can still walk

Curves progress rapidly after loss of ambulation while respiratory function declines, so fusion, often to the pelvis, is done early in the curve's course. Long-term corticosteroids reduce the incidence of scoliosis. Anaesthetic planning must address cardiomyopathy and avoid suxamethonium and volatile agents because of the risk of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia.
In a child with myelomeningocele, which functional neurological level is most associated with community ambulation using ankle–foot orthoses?
Low lumbar (L4, with functioning quadriceps) and below
Any level, provided bracing is good

Quadriceps function (L3–L4) is the key to walking; sacral levels walk nearly normally and thoracic levels mostly use wheelchairs. Rapid progression of scoliosis or new spasticity should prompt assessment for shunt malfunction, tethered cord or hydromyelia, and all patients need latex precautions.
A 4-year-old girl has had a painless swollen knee for 2 months. She is ANA-positive and has no systemic features. Which surveillance is most important?

Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the most common subtype, and young, ANA-positive girls have the highest risk of asymptomatic anterior uveitis, which can cause blindness. Chronic knee inflammation can also cause overgrowth and leg-length discrepancy. Intra-articular corticosteroid is commonly used.

A 10-year-old boy has a congenital leg-length discrepancy of 3 cm. A rapid method predicts the discrepancy at skeletal maturity by multiplying the current discrepancy by an age- and sex-specific factor. This is the:

Congenital discrepancies grow in proportion to the limb, so the multiplier applies directly. As a rough guide, a predicted final discrepancy under about 2 cm is managed with a shoe raise, about 2–5 cm with epiphysiodesis of the longer limb, and larger discrepancies with lengthening.
Which physis contributes most to the length of the lower limb?

The distal femur provides about 70% of femoral growth (about 9–10 mm a year) and the proximal tibia about 55–60% of tibial growth (about 6 mm a year). In the upper limb, the proximal humerus and distal radius contribute most, summarised as 'towards the knee, away from the elbow'.
A child has isolated hemihypertrophy causing a leg-length discrepancy. Which screening is recommended?
Serial abdominal ultrasound for Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma

Isolated hemihypertrophy and Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome carry an increased risk of embryonal tumours, so abdominal ultrasound is repeated about every 3 months in early childhood, often with serum alpha-fetoprotein for hepatoblastoma. Limb-length management follows the usual principles.
In thumb duplication (radial polydactyly), the most common Wassel type is:

Reconstruction, usually around 1 year of age, removes the smaller (usually radial) thumb while preserving and reattaching its radial collateral ligament and thenar insertion to the retained thumb, and centralises the tendons. Simple excision without reconstruction leaves an unstable, deviated thumb.
A 2-year-old has a thumb fixed in flexion at the IP joint, with a palpable nodule at the base of the thumb. Diagnosis and usual management:
Paediatric trigger thumb; observation or splinting first, then A1 pulley release if it persists
Thumb-in-palm deformity of cerebral palsy; botulinum toxin

The nodule (Notta node) is a thickening of FPL that cannot pass the A1 pulley. Many resolve spontaneously, and release of the A1 pulley is curative for persistent cases. The radial digital nerve lies close to the incision and must be protected.
A 7-year-old develops painful torticollis with the head tilted and rotated (a 'cock-robin' posture) a week after tonsillitis. Dynamic CT shows C1 fixed in rotation on C2. Diagnosis:

Inflammation spreading from the pharynx loosens the C1–C2 ligaments. Early cases are treated with a collar and NSAIDs, cases lasting more than about a week with halter traction, and chronic irreducible cases with halo reduction or C1–C2 fusion. The Fielding classification grades the C1 displacement.
A 6-year-old has painless flat feet. The arch reappears when he stands on tiptoe and the heel swings into varus. Best management:

Flexible flatfoot is a normal variant in most children, and orthotics do not change arch development. Check for a tight Achilles tendon, which can make a flexible flatfoot painful. A rigid flatfoot that does not correct on tiptoe suggests tarsal coalition or another pathology.
Resection of a physeal bar with interposition of fat or cement is most appropriate when the bar:
Involves more than 75% of the physis
Is in a skeletally mature patient
Involves less than about 50% of the physis and at least 2 years of growth remain
Causes no angular deformity or shortening

CT or MRI mapping determines the size and type of bar (central, peripheral or linear). Larger bars, or bars in children with little growth left, are treated with completion epiphysiodesis (with or without contralateral epiphysiodesis), osteotomy or lengthening.
Flexible titanium elastic nails for a femoral shaft fracture in an older child have a higher rate of malunion and complications when the child weighs more than about:

Heavier children, especially around 49 kg or more, and length-unstable comminuted fractures do less well with elastic nails. Alternatives include a lateral-entry rigid trochanteric nail in adolescents and submuscular bridge plating. Each elastic nail should fill about 40% of the canal.
Why is antegrade femoral nailing through a piriformis fossa entry point avoided in children with open proximal femoral physes?
It risks damage to branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery, causing femoral head AVN

The lateral ascending branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery run in the trochanteric fossa to supply the femoral head. Lateral trochanteric entry nails avoid this and are used in adolescents. An entry point through the greater trochanteric apophysis can also disturb its growth.
A woman at moderate fracture risk has taken oral alendronate for 5 years, has had no fractures and her hip BMD is now above the osteoporotic range. A reasonable next step is to:
Consider a drug holiday and reassess fracture risk after about 1–3 years

Bisphosphonates are retained in bone and keep acting after they are stopped, while long-term use increases the risk of atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw. Higher-risk patients, such as those with previous vertebral fractures, may continue for up to about 10 years orally or 6 years intravenously.
Compared with postmenopausal osteoporosis, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis:
Causes fractures only after 10 years of use
Causes fractures at higher BMD values, particularly in trabecular bone such as the vertebrae
Is driven mainly by increased bone formation

Glucocorticoids reduce bone formation through osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis and transiently increase resorption. Fracture risk rises within a few months of starting and is dose-dependent, so BMD underestimates risk. Bisphosphonates are first line, and teriparatide is an option in high-risk patients.
The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is:

A single adenoma accounts for most cases, with raised calcium, raised or inappropriately normal PTH and low or normal phosphate. Multigland hyperplasia occurs in MEN syndromes, carcinoma is rare, and chronic kidney disease causes secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Which drug commonly raises serum urate and can precipitate an attack of gout after orthopaedic surgery?

Thiazide and loop diuretics reduce renal urate excretion; low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin and pyrazinamide have similar effects. Postoperative gout is common because of dehydration, fasting and stress. Losartan modestly lowers urate, and allopurinol and febuxostat are xanthine oxidase inhibitors.
Which serological test is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?

Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific and predict erosive disease. Rheumatoid factor is less specific and is found in other conditions and some healthy older people. ANA is typical of SLE, and HLA-B27 of the spondyloarthropathies.
Radiographs of an adult's hands show joint space narrowing and hook-like osteophytes of the second and third MCP joints, with chondrocalcinosis. Which condition should be tested for?

Haemochromatosis arthropathy classically affects the second and third MCP joints and is associated with CPPD deposition. Check ferritin and transferrin saturation, and HFE genotype. Venesection treats iron overload but does not reverse the arthropathy.
A child with short, malformed great toes develops painful soft-tissue swellings in the neck and back after minor knocks, which later ossify. Which action must be avoided?
NSAIDs or a short course of corticosteroids for flare-ups
Biopsy or surgical excision of the swellings

This is fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, caused by an activating ACVR1 mutation. Trauma, including biopsy, surgery and intramuscular injections, triggers further heterotopic ossification, which progressively locks the joints. The great toe malformation at birth is the key early clue.
In osteonecrosis of the femoral head, a subchondral 'crescent sign' on radiographs indicates:
A subchondral fracture, so collapse has begun

The crescent is a lucent line beneath the subchondral plate from fracture through necrotic bone (ARCO stage 3). Head-preserving procedures such as core decompression work best before collapse, so the crescent sign marks a poorer prognosis and often a move towards arthroplasty.
On T2-weighted MRI of early femoral head osteonecrosis, the 'double-line sign' consists of:
An inner bright line of granulation tissue and an outer dark line of sclerotic bone
A joint effusion with marrow oedema

The double-line sign marks the reactive interface around the necrotic segment and is highly specific; MRI is the most sensitive test. Risk factors include corticosteroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, SLE and Gaucher disease. The other hip is often affected, so both are imaged.
A commercial diver develops hip pain years after many deep dives. Radiographs show osteonecrosis of the femoral and humeral heads. The mechanism is:
Nitrogen bubbles occluding bone vessels (dysbaric osteonecrosis)

Nitrogen dissolves in fatty marrow at depth and forms bubbles during decompression, blocking vessels. Lesions occur in the femoral and humeral heads and as medullary infarcts in long bones, and may appear long after exposure. Prevention relies on proper decompression schedules.
An infant has bilateral, symmetrical destruction of the medial proximal tibial metaphyses with periostitis of several long bones. This 'Wimberger sign' suggests:

Congenital syphilis causes metaphysitis, diaphyseal periostitis and painful pseudoparalysis (Parrot). The Wimberger sign of syphilis differs from the Wimberger ring of scurvy, which is a sclerotic rim around the epiphysis. Late features include sabre tibia and painless bilateral knee effusions (Clutton joints). Treatment is penicillin.
A farmer from an endemic area has a multiloculated lytic lesion of the pelvis without periosteal reaction, and MRI shows multiple small cysts within a larger cyst. Most likely diagnosis and organism:

Bone hydatid disease is uncommon, favours the spine and pelvis, and spreads through bone like a slow, unencapsulated tumour. Diagnosis uses imaging and serology. Treatment is wide excision with albendazole cover, avoiding spillage, which risks anaphylaxis and dissemination; recurrence is common.

A 12-year-old has a painful, hard swelling of the mandible after a dental infection. Radiographs show marked cortical thickening with layered periosteal new bone but no suppuration or sequestrum. This is:

Garré osteomyelitis is a chronic, low-grade, non-suppurative infection that stimulates periosteal bone formation, most often in the mandible of children and young adults. Treatment addresses the source, such as the infected tooth. Caffey disease occurs in infants under about 6 months, and Ewing sarcoma must be excluded when the features are atypical.

A diabetic rice farmer from South or Southeast Asia develops septic arthritis and multifocal abscesses during the monsoon. Gram-negative bacilli with bipolar 'safety-pin' staining are grown. Organism and treatment:
Burkholderia pseudomallei; intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem, then prolonged oral co-trimoxazole

Melioidosis is acquired from soil and water and diabetes is the main risk factor. Bone and joint infection needs drainage, an intensive intravenous phase of at least 2 weeks and an eradication phase of several months, because relapse is common.
In children with MRSA acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, which complication is particularly associated and should be looked for?
Pathological fracture within the first day
Deep vein thrombosis and septic pulmonary emboli

MRSA strains, especially those producing Panton–Valentine leukocidin, cause more severe sepsis, multifocal disease, subperiosteal abscesses and venous thrombosis near the infected bone, which can embolise to the lungs. Severe cases need surgical drainage and an anti-MRSA antibiotic chosen by local resistance patterns.
In adults, native-joint bacterial septic arthritis most often affects the:

About half of adult cases involve the knee. Risk factors include rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, joint prostheses, older age and intravenous drug use, which is linked to unusual sites such as the sternoclavicular and sacroiliac joints. S. aureus is the main organism, and treatment combines joint washout or repeated aspiration with antibiotics.
In a diabetic foot, which MRI feature favours osteomyelitis over acute Charcot neuroarthropathy?
Periarticular oedema involving several midfoot joints
Marrow change centred on a single bone directly beneath an ulcer or sinus tract
Subchondral cysts at several tarsometatarsal joints
Joint effusions without any skin ulcer

Osteomyelitis in diabetes almost always spreads from an adjacent ulcer, typically under the forefoot or heel, and involves one bone. Charcot arthropathy is periarticular, involves several joints, favours the midfoot and occurs without an ulcer. The two can coexist, and biopsy settles doubt.
